principles.quote: Wouldn’t it be great if when you went to buy a computer—or after you bought a computer—if you had any questions, you could ask a Genius?

principles.text: Back front-line staff with the company's deepest expertise, so no customer question goes unanswered.
principles.quote: if that person doesn't know the answer, they've got a hotline to call us in Cupertino at Apple headquarters, where we have somebody who does.

principles.text: Serve the whole ecosystem around your product, not only your own products.
principles.quote: We decided carrying our own products wasn’t enough, so we’re carrying six digital camcorders, six digital cameras, six MP3 players, and six handheld organizers.

principles.text: In a crisis, put people's safety first and tell the team to lean on each other.
principles.quote: Please take the time you need for your families, and please lean on one another. Together, we will all get through this.

sources.title: Steve Jobs's emails to himself (2003): what moved him in music, and how he saw Pixar's Golden Age
sources.originalTitle: Make Something Wonderful: Emails to himself: This song moves me like few others, and Golden Age (2003)
sources.summary: Two private notes Jobs wrote in 2003: a playlist writeup about songs that made him cry or recalled his childhood, and talk prep celebrating Pixar's Golden Age. They show his taste, emotional honesty, and view that great work comes from the maturing of people.

principles.text: Pixar's greatness was fueled by people growing into mastery, not by any single product.
principles.quote: Our real Golden Age is being fueled by the maturing of our people.

principles.text: Celebrate a track record of original work, and judge success against the history of the field.
principles.quote: All original Pixar stories. Our track record of 4 for 4, and hopefully 5 for 5, is unparalleled in the history of animation, and indeed in the history of film.

principles.text: Build a bench: watch for the next generation of leaders coming up behind the current one.
principles.quote: And I see more directors and producers coming right behind them.

principles.text: Pause to recognize that you are living through a great moment while it is happening.
principles.quote: Tonight is a night for celebration, but don’t forget to pause for a moment and realize that this is what it feels like to be living in—and creating—a Golden Age.

principles.text: Great art connects to personal, emotional truth; his taste was guided by what moved him deeply.
principles.quote: Maybe it’s because I’m adopted, but this song moves me like few others.

principles.text: Technology and the arts meet through craft: lyrics and music he loved shaped his sense of quality.
principles.quote: I had not listened to much Jackson Browne at that time, and was just blown away by the lyrics.

sources.title: How Steve Jobs learned from Robert Noyce: cold-calling legends and hiring smarter people
sources.originalTitle: Make Something Wonderful: Interview with Leslie Berlin (2003)
sources.summary: In a 2003 interview, Jobs reflects on his mentor Robert Noyce, the "soul of Intel." He explains how he cold-called Valley legends for lunch, why a senior leader's job is recruiting, direction and inspiration rather than doing the work, why optimism and passion sustain innovation, and why history and succession matter.

principles.text: Cold-call the people you admire and ask to learn from them; most will say yes.
principles.quote: I just called them up and I said, “Look, I’m young and I’m trying to run with this company. I’m just wondering if I could buy you lunch once a quarter and pick your brain.”

principles.text: Hire people smarter than you, including younger ones, instead of doing their work.
principles.quote: If you’re smart, you’re hiring twenty-five-year-olds who are smarter than you. You know things that they don’t know, and they know things that you don’t know, and it all works.

principles.text: A leader's job is to recruit, set direction, and inspire, not design the product.
principles.quote: His job was to, number one, recruit; number two, set an overall direction; and number three, you know, inspire and cajole and persuade.

principles.text: Innovation needs optimism and real passion, because it is extremely hard.
principles.quote: It’s optimism and passion, because it’s really hard. And if you don’t really, really care about what you’re doing, you’re gonna give up if you’re a sane person

principles.text: To understand the present you must understand how it got here; there is humanity under the dry history.
principles.quote: There’s a human drama to most everything. You look at it sometimes, and it seems dry as history. But if you peel the onion, there’s humanity underneath.

principles.text: Great leaders plan succession and let go, so the company is not a one-man show.
principles.quote: He understood how important it was to have a succession, to keep the company going, not have it just be a one-man show.

sources.title: Make Something Wonderful: Steve's 2003 Stanford GSB talk on hiring A players and management by values
sources.originalTitle: Make Something Wonderful: Speech at Stanford's Graduate School of Business (2003)
sources.summary: In a 2003 talk to MBA students, Steve compares running Apple and Pixar and explains why Apple built its own retail stores. His core lessons: hire people far better than you, since the dynamic range of talent is enormous. Lead by "management by values", getting everyone to agree on the destination, and treat recruiting as the most important thing a leader does.

principles.text: Hire people better than you; the talent gap between average and best is huge.
principles.quote: The most important lesson I ever learned was that you have to hire people better than you are.

principles.text: A small team of great people can outdo hundreds or thousands of average ones.
principles.quote: I saw a team of fifty people do something that literally hundreds, or thousands, of people at other companies couldn’t do.

principles.text: Manage by values: find people who want the same things you do, then get out of their way.
principles.quote: What that means is you find people that want the same things you want, and then just get the hell out of their way.

principles.text: Agree on the destination, not the route; let each generation argue about how to get there.
principles.quote: So that each generation can argue anew about the best way to get to San Diego, and they’re not just taking your footsteps on how you got there.

principles.text: Make great products the goal; profit follows. Reversing the order makes things fall apart.
principles.quote: “We want to make a bunch of money, and so, OK, to do that, we’re going to have to make some good personal computers.” But it didn’t work. It never works.

principles.text: Recruiting is the most important thing a leader does; finding the right people is half the battle.
principles.quote: recruiting is the most important thing that you do. Finding the right people—that’s half the battle.

sources.title: How Steve Jobs drafted the Stanford commencement address: ideas from his emails to himself
sources.originalTitle: Make Something Wonderful: Drafting the Stanford Commencement Address (2005)
sources.summary: Steve's emails to himself while drafting the 2005 Stanford speech show the raw ideas behind it: curiosity, surrounding yourself with smarter people, recognizing life-changing chance, investing in yourself, and using death and story to make big choices. It also shows his process, working on it for six months and refining it the morning he gave it.

principles.text: Surround yourself with people smarter than you, even from a different walk of life; that's how you get smarter and deeper.
principles.quote: the first piece of advice I want to give you is to try to always surround yourself with people smarter than you. This is how you get smarter and deeper.

principles.text: A great teacher holds the flashlight just long enough for you to find your own.
principles.quote: a teacher is someone who stands with you in the dark and holds their flashlight just long enough for you to find your own flashlight.

principles.text: You can't plan for the people who change your life, so recognize them and have the courage to grab on.
principles.quote: You can’t plan to meet the people who will change your life. It just happens.

principles.text: Invest in yourself and in going for it, not in nicer cars or apartments; you have little to lose when you start.
principles.quote: rather than invest in better cars, or better apartments, or our bank accounts, we decided to invest in ourselves.

principles.text: Remembering you'll be dead soon frees you to follow your heart and ignore others' expectations and fear of failure.
principles.quote: all of the expectations and standards and restrictions of others and society mean nothing in the end.

principles.text: Treat your life as a story in the making and picture looking back on it to choose the path that makes your heart sing.
principles.quote: if you can remember that your life is a story in the making, it will help you make those important decisions.

sources.title: Steve Jobs at Stanford 2005: connect the dots, love your work, remember death
sources.originalTitle: Make Something Wonderful: Commencement Address at Stanford University (2005)
sources.summary: Jobs tells three stories: dropping in on a calligraphy class that later shaped the Mac's typography, being fired from Apple and finding it freeing, and facing cancer. The lessons: trust your curiosity and intuition, do only work you love, use mortality to cut through fear, and stay hungry and foolish.

principles.text: You can only connect the dots looking backward, so trust that curiosity and intuition will pay off later.
principles.quote: you can’t connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backwards. So you have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future.

principles.text: Follow curiosity even without practical payoff; it can become the foundation of great design.
principles.quote: None of this had even a hope of any practical application in my life. But ten years later, when we were designing the first Macintosh computer, it all came back to me.

principles.text: Great work requires loving what you do; keep looking and never settle.
principles.quote: the only way to be truly satisfied is to do what you believe is great work. And the only way to do great work is to love what you do. If you haven’t found it yet, keep looking. Don’t settle.

principles.text: Setbacks can free you: failure replaces the weight of success with the lightness of being a beginner.
principles.quote: The heaviness of being successful was replaced by the lightness of being a beginner again, less sure about everything. It freed me to enter one of the most creative periods of my life.

principles.text: Ask each morning if today were your last, would you do what you're about to do; change course if the answer is no too often.
principles.quote: If today were the last day of my life, would I want to do what I am about to do today?” And whenever the answer has been “No” for too many days in a row, I know I need to change something.

principles.text: Don't live someone else's life or let others' opinions drown out your inner voice.
principles.quote: Your time is limited, so don’t waste it living someone else’s life. Don’t be trapped by dogma—which is living with the results of other people’s thinking.

sources.title: How Steve Jobs framed the iPhone: fix what everyone hates, make complex tech easy to use
sources.originalTitle: Make Something Wonderful: Please reset the iPod (2005), Speech to Apple Employees and Speech at Macworld (2007)
sources.summary: Jobs explains why Apple built the iPhone: not from market research but because everyone hated their phones. He says Apple's core competence is making complex technology easy and self-discoverable, and at Macworld he lays out why fixed buttons give way to multitouch, plus the hardware-software integration behind it.

principles.text: Build what you and your friends actually want, not what market research or spreadsheets suggest.
principles.quote: And it wasn’t driven by a bunch of market research or financial spreadsheets about how big certain markets were. It wasn’t driven by that at all. It was driven by the fact that we all hated our phones.

principles.text: Features nobody can discover might as well not exist; make complex technology easy and self-discoverable.
principles.quote: And what our competence is, is making complex technology easy to use and self-discoverable.

principles.text: Aim to make a contribution by making something truly great that you love.
principles.quote: We thought we could make a contribution by making something truly great that we loved.

principles.text: Aim for a leapfrog product that is both smarter and easier, rather than trading one off against the other.
principles.quote: What we want to do is make a leapfrog product that is way smarter than any mobile device has ever been and super easy to use.

principles.text: Remove fixed controls so the interface can adapt to each application and to future ideas.
principles.quote: Well, every application wants a slightly different user interface, a slightly optimized set of buttons, just for it.

principles.text: Serious software people should make their own hardware; integrate the two.
principles.quote: “People who are really serious about software should make their own hardware.”

sources.title: Steve Jobs's late notes: Pixar-style products for everybody, gratitude, and organ donation (2007-2010)
sources.originalTitle: Make Something Wonderful: Late notes and speeches (2007 to 2010): Art Levinson, the press, the iPad, Lucile Packard, emails to himself
sources.summary: A collection of Steve's late emails and speeches. He explains why Apple designs products for everybody the way Pixar makes films, says a company is only as good as its next product, and reflects on how dependent every person is on the work of others. He also pushes organ donation with "one simple question."

principles.text: Design for everybody, not a narrow target demographic, the way Pixar makes films for every layer of the family.
principles.quote: we don’t think, “Oh, well, our target audience is fifteen to twenty-nine, male.” We don’t think that way. We think about making a great product for just about everybody.

principles.text: Software lets one great device be tailored to do almost anything.
principles.quote: the beauty of the products we make is they can be tailored with software to do almost anything.

principles.text: Past wins, even passing Microsoft, don't matter. You are only as good as your next amazing product.
principles.quote: Walt Disney used to say to his team: “We’re only as good as our next picture.” Well, we’re only as good as our next amazing new product.

principles.text: Take a moment to reflect on success, but know that glory is fleeting and go back to work.
principles.quote: Stocks go up and down, and things may be different tomorrow, but I thought it was worth a moment of reflection today.

principles.text: Meaningful work is work you can proudly explain to your kids.
principles.quote: We can say, “I worked on our next-generation iPad. You know, the ones that you use in school.” And that’s a really wonderful thing.

principles.text: Every person depends on the creations of countless others, so love and admire humanity and be grateful.
principles.quote: I love and admire my species, living and dead, and am totally dependent on them for my life and well being.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At the 1983 International Design Conference in Aspen, Jobs frames the personal computer as a new medium, pleads with designers to make it beautiful instead of another piece of junk, and explains Apple's push to put a great computer in a book. He also describes hiring exceptional people, keeping teams small and flat, and bringing the liberal arts into technology.

chunks.heading: Computers as a new medium, and why design matters
chunks.text:
- Steve describes a computer as "a simple machine" where "the gears, the Pistons have been replaced with electrons." Computers are adaptive, new, and "really dumb": the raw instructions are trivial (fetch a number, add two numbers, test if it's bigger than zero), but they run fast enough to look like magic.
- His analogy: if he could move 100 times faster than anyone in the room, he could run out, grab a bouquet of spring flowers and snap his fingers, and "you'd all think I was a magician."
- Over the last 20 years, people have built higher levels of abstraction on top of these instructions. "Could you go get some flowers" replaces "Left Foot, Right Foot, extend hand."
- At the time he gave the talk, the oldest person with a computer science degree was 39, and the average age of professionals at Apple was under 30.

chunks.heading: Fractional horsepower computing: why Apple exists
chunks.text:
- Steve uses the electric motor as a history of computers. First came one huge motor, cost-justified only for giant applications. Then one motor shared through shafts and belts across 15 to 20 workstations. Then the fractional horsepower motor, which put power exactly where needed. He says a household has about 55 of them.
- Computers followed the same path: ENIAC in 1947 for ballistic calculations, then time sharing in the 1960s (one big computer split across many terminal users), then the personal computer.
- "The reason Apple exists is because we stumbled on to fractional horsepower Computing 5 years before anybody else."
- People looked at the 13 lb Apple and asked where the computer was. He told them it was the whole computer. The personal computer was invented in 1976. The industry would ship over 3 million in 1983 and, by 1986, more computers than automobiles in the US.

chunks.heading: A call to designers: make the new object great
chunks.text:
- Steve says computers "look like garbage." The great product designers are off designing cars and buildings, and hardly any design computers.
- He argues that the 3 million units this year and 10 million in 1986 will sell "whether they look like a piece of [junk] or they look great," because demand is huge, and "it doesn't cost any more money to make it look great."
- Computers will sit in every workplace, school and home. People will spend two or three hours a day with them, longer than in a car, so industrial design, software design and interaction deserve at least the care given to automobiles, "if not a lot more."
- He says most of life's objects (cars, TVs, audio, watches, cameras, bicycles, calculators) are not designed in America: "we've blown it" on both industry and design.
- Computers and society are "out on a first date" in the 80s, so there is a chance to make them beautiful and communicate something through the design of the objects.
- Apple would spend over $100 million on media advertising in 12 months, and generate tens of millions of dollars of brochures and posters. He says this "can either be great or it can be lousy and we need help."

chunks.heading: Every medium shapes the communication, and new media start by imitating old ones
chunks.text:
- A medium shapes not just the message but the process of communication. His example: the telephone requires both people present, while electronic mail lets someone retrieve a drawing at midnight, three days later, or from another city.
- New media fall back on old habits. Early TV was radio with a camera pointed at it, and it took most of the 1950s to find its own form. He cites the JFK funeral and the Apollo landing as moments that were not possible on radio.
- The video disc (55,000 images per side, or an hour of video) is mostly used for movies. His counterexample is the MIT Aspen Movie Map: every street and intersection photographed, a touch screen to walk forward, look left or right, enter shops, and switch between all four seasons.
- Computers are in the "I Love Lucy stage": business accounting in COBOL, as TV copied radio. Lisa is starting to break out. He has no drawing talent, but with LisaDraw can erase, move, shrink, grow, texture and airbrush images, then paste them into documents and email them.
- He expects the first phase of putting these tools into society to last about 15 years, and that period is a chance "to do it great or to do it so-so."

chunks.heading: Software captures underlying principles, not just experiences
chunks.text:
- A computer program has no physical manifestation. It is "simply ideas expressed on paper."
- TV can recreate a set of recorded experiences, like the JFK funeral or Neil Armstrong on the moon. Programming instead "captures the underlying principles of an experience," which can generate thousands of different experiences that obey those laws.
- Examples: a Pong game follows gravity and angular momentum, so no two games are the same. In Hammurabi, seven-year-olds act as king of ancient Sumeria and manage wheat, land, feeding and planting. They play for hours with a crude macroeconomic model and learn from it. He says models must keep getting more sophisticated.
- His vision: books were great because they went from Aristotle to the reader with no intermediary, but "you can't ask Aristotle a question." Maybe a future Aristotle will carry a machine for life, and someone could later ask it what he would have said. "Maybe we won't get the right answer, but maybe we will, and that's really exciting to me and that's one of the reasons I'm doing what I'm doing."

chunks.heading: Apple's strategy: the computer in a book, and "liberal arts" in the machine
chunks.text:
- Strategy: "put an incredibly great computer in a book that you can carry around with you that you can learn how to use in 20 minutes," with a radio link, within the decade. It is not yet technically possible.
- Three options: do nothing (too impatient), put a "piece of garbage computer in a book" (competitors do that), or design the computer they want to put in the book eventually. That is Lisa: breadbox-sized and $10,000 now, sold out for the next year, with an office market that pays for development.
- Next steps he projects: a shoebox-sized machine at about $2,500, then a book-sized one under $1,000, within five to seven years.
- Existing computers used ugly type (an "i" as wide as a "W"), few fonts, and no graphics mixed with text. Lisa has proportionally spaced text, 30 to 40 fonts, about 80 dots per inch on screen and up to 300 on a laser printer. He wants 600 to 800 dpi on a laser film printer. "We're solving the problems of injecting some liberal arts into these computers."
- Goal: in three or four years no college student writes a paper without one, "just like they will not think of going to a science class without a calculator today," and people think "wasn't this the way it always was."
- Computers should be easy to use: "We've got to get away from programming, because people don't want to program computers, people want to use computers." Generic programs (word processors, databases, spreadsheets) do about 90% of the work, with graphical programming next. He notes that the HP-35 and reverse Polish notation or a Casio watch with 18 alarms would have confused people 10 years earlier, so technical literacy rises over time.

chunks.heading: Building a company on great people
chunks.text:
- Every professional at Apple owns stock. He had "never heard the word labor or management mentioned at Apple," and says it works like a union of everyone pursuing the same goals. Turnover has been under 5% since inception.
- A deeper motive: most of what we use (clothes, food, language, mathematics) was made by others. "You're constantly taking, and the ability to put something back into that pool of Human Experience is extremely neat."
- Hiring: "We believe in the phenomenon of great people": some people "can run circles around five pretty good people," and those are who Apple wants. They are idiosyncratic, "the artists of the world."
- Apple was approaching $1 billion in sales with under 5,000 people worldwide. Steve says they always hired people far better than the current job needed, because within six months the job grows. They hire people to tell Apple what to do: figure out what is needed, say what it costs, and do it. He wants an environment where people don't have to convince 30 others.
- The day someone decides they can't make a difference "is the day we've lost." Anyone can see him or John Sculley within a day or two. He observes that the Catholic church, the oldest and largest organization, has about four layers of management, so Apple needs no more than four and usually has about three.
- Starting with nothing, "you always can shoot for the moon, you have nothing to lose." Success tempts people into "cover your ass mode" and conservatism. The company gambled everything on Lisa for three and a half years, using the best and the brightest, and recruited people whose employers wouldn't take the risk. "Who do I have to convince to do that? Nobody, just go do it."
- He describes the culture: engineers arrive around 11, play ping pong, work hard, play volleyball around 4, work until 2 or 3 a.m. "They're a lot closer to artists" than the computer-nerd stereotype.

chunks.heading: Connecting computers, information, and education
chunks.text:
- Networks: Xerox PARC linked about 100 computers on a local area network, and mailing lists multiplied: volleyball, Chinese cooking, until "there were more lists than people." He predicts networking will bring people together around special interests. He estimates five years to solve office networking and 10 to 15 for the home.
- On privacy, he is more concerned about the ability to turn information into knowledge than about giant databases. Tools for filtering are centralized, and the answer is to distribute that intelligence. His example: filtering congressional testimony on gun control, then emailing a nasty letter to his congressman.
- "Kids Can't Wait": California's Commission on Industrial Innovation found that about 44% of new California jobs in the 1980s would come directly or indirectly from high technology, and education was the biggest obstacle. Apple offered to give a computer to each of America's roughly 100,000 schools (about $50 million). Congress would pay 40% if Apple paid 10% (Apple made $40 million in 1981, so this was a significant bet). Senator Bob Dole killed the federal version, but California passed a law, and Apple would roll out 10,000 computers, one free to every California school, starting the next month. It won't fundamentally change the problem, but it avoids a computer "have-not" split.
- He says Apple doesn't do such things as a public service: "we do them because we think they ought to be done." Over half of GNP already comes from the information business, and laid-off auto workers must be retrained or "they're going to burn the cities down."
- Software distribution: there are 20,000 Apple II programs and about 2,000 IBM PC programs, and buyers don't know what to buy. Records have the radio station for free sampling, so software needs a "software radio station": send programs over phone lines, offer 30 seconds free or five screenshots, then buy with a Visa number.
- Opportunity: there were a million Apple IIs. A real-estate calculation program sold at $100 (dealer takes $50, $25 to make) to 10% of owners would yield about $2.5 million in profit, using under $10,000 of equipment (the figures in the transcript are garbled; the point is that a small developer can profit hugely). He mentions a 13-year-old who started Aristotle Software and was earning about $4,000 a week from three game programs.
- Voice recognition is "the better part of a decade away," because understanding language in context is much harder than recognizing words.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At MIT Sloan in 1992, Jobs explains NeXT's strategy: attack operational productivity with object-oriented software, pair it with hardware so a direct sales force can create demand, and run the company through consensus among A-player executives. He also shares lessons from Apple, manufacturing, and technology windows.

chunks.heading: Operational apps are the next big wave in desktop computing
chunks.text:
- Steve cites Paul Strassman's *The Business Value of Computers*: successful and unsuccessful companies all spend about 2% of revenue on information technology. The difference is where the money goes. Less successful firms spend most on management productivity; more successful ones spend most on operational productivity applications.
- He concedes PCs and Macs only ever attacked management productivity, and that he "spent the first ten years of my life" on it. You can't buy an off-the-shelf app to run a hospital or do stock trading.
- His history: the 60s and 70s meant mainframes, terminals and COBOL programmers; the 80s changed nothing. Only two or three years earlier did front offices start downsizing to servers, Sybase or Oracle databases and Sun workstations, spending about two years writing apps such as Wall Street trading apps.
- New products in financial services need an idea, a sales force and a custom app to make the product real. Without the app there is no product.
- He compares this to desktop publishing in 1985, which nobody understood at first. His bet is that operational apps are the next big revolution and are more horizontal than they look.

chunks.heading: You often don't know your competitive advantage until customers tell you
chunks.text:
- With the Macintosh, Apple anticipated bitmap displays and laser printers, but never desktop publishing. That became the Mac's compelling advantage, "four or five times better than anything else". It arrived 9 to 12 months after launch, and Apple changed its whole marketing and business strategy to focus on it.
- Desktop publishing became the "Trojan horse" that got the Mac into corporate America.
- NeXTSTEP followed the same pattern. It was aimed at shrink-wrap developers such as Lotus, Adobe and WordPerfect, and was a success there.
- In early 1991 big companies told NeXT, "you don't understand what you've got". The same software that lets Lotus build apps 5 to 10 times faster does that for in-house mission-critical apps. The message took about three months to sink in.
- NeXT changed its sales and marketing strategy that summer. Revenue grew about 4x last year and he expects about 2x this year.
- On Wall Street, building a product in 90 days instead of a competitor's two years means eight new products to their one.

chunks.heading: Software is the sustainable advantage, hardware is not
chunks.text:
- Hardware churns every 18 months. If you are lucky you build something 1.5 to 2 times better than a competitor's, and it lasts about six months.
- Software takes much longer to catch up with. Microsoft took eight or nine years to catch up with the Mac, "and it's arguable whether they've even caught up".
- He estimates NeXT's first true competitor is four to five years away. That gives NeXT roughly 3 to 4 years to grow a $1-2 billion company so it can compete on scale (salespeople, ad budgets) with Sun.
- His competitor read:
  - Sun's Solaris has no objects and is falling behind in software.
  - Microsoft NT is "better plumbing for Windows", with the worst development environment ever invented and no object orientation.
  - Taligent is the first true competitor, expected around 1995. If it executes, it will have by the mid-90s roughly what NeXT has today.
- IBM and Apple endorsing object-oriented programming helps NeXT, because NeXT is the only one shipping it now.
- NeXTSTEP is an operating environment more than an operating system, and the UNIX is only about 10% of it.
- Developers don't write code faster on NeXTSTEP, but a given app takes about 20% of the code. "The code that's the fastest to write, the code that's the easiest to maintain and the code that never breaks is the code you don't write."
- NeXT ships six years' worth of objects. Independent third parties selling objects (not system software or apps) had begun to appear, about ten of them. He thinks that will be big.
- He advises software startups to write objects for other developers rather than polished shrink-wrapped apps. Marketing a breakthrough spreadsheet on mainstream platforms would cost $15-50 million just to rise above the noise.

chunks.heading: Why NeXT is both a hardware and a software company
chunks.text:
- NeXT was porting NeXTSTEP to the Intel 486, shipping in September or October, for $995. This answered customer requests. Intel and Novell were helping because they feared Microsoft and saw NeXTSTEP as the only thing that could challenge it in system software for years.
- Sun customers wanted it on Sun hardware. Sun said it would rather "stick needles in their eyes". Steve says NeXT, being customer-driven, will probably do what customers ask.
- He expects to sell less than 100% of NeXTSTEP hardware but more hardware in absolute terms, and would be happy to sell 20-25% of NeXTSTEP hardware.
- The deeper reason is distribution. Computer stores can fulfill demand but can't create it, and the more revolutionary a product, the less the channel helps. Phone and Federal Express are making the store channel obsolete.
- NeXT's answer was a direct sales force of about 130 professionals in the US, spending 90% of their time on NeXTSTEP software and 10% on hardware. You can't fund that with $500 software packages, but you can with $5,000 average selling prices.
- Therefore, he says, no more system software companies will succeed on software alone: "we've got to be a hardware company in order to make our software business succeed".
- He expects a fracturing as NeXTSTEP spreads, comparable to when the Mac arrived. Other environments will absorb its breakthroughs and things will balance out over time.

chunks.heading: Manufacturing as a competitive weapon
chunks.text:
- At Apple he led the effort to build the Mac factory. His mistake there: the two big pieces of automation, a small-parts storage and retrieval system and a burn-in system, were just "high tech warehouses". Warehouses hide defects, delay the quality feedback loop with vendors, and tie up money. NeXT's factory has no warehouses and uses true just-in-time delivery to the point of use.
- He uses Stephen Wheelwright's five-stage scale, from manufacturing as a "necessary evil" to manufacturing as a source of competitive advantage. He applies it to software too: most computer companies see software as a necessary evil, while only NeXT, Apple and Microsoft sit in stage five.
- NeXT treated the factory as a software problem, and its first factory hires were software engineers, persuaded to move from R&D with bonuses and a promise they could go back. Robot generations:
  - First: bought turnkey.
  - Second: specced the hardware, wrote the software on NeXT machines.
  - Third: built the robot hardware itself, which turned out cheaper than buying.
- Shipping early depends on parallelism. Manufacturing is involved from day one, and engineering hasn't built a wire-wrap or other prototype in two years. Prototypes are built on the actual production line at lot size one, with CAD data flowing over a T1 to a plant about 15 minutes away. No technology change means no accumulated knowledge is thrown away.
- Manufacturing people are paid the same as R&D, have the same offices, equipment and computers, and can move in both directions. For the first few years manufacturing had more PhDs than design engineering.
- He claims NeXT machines cost roughly half of Sun's and are built in Fremont, California, on the most automated factory in the industry. Canon, NeXT's Japanese partner, rates it a high-quality supplier.
- Suppliers own getting zero-defect material to the factory on time. NeXT pushes statistical quality data back to suppliers (Motorola is a key one). "Our money doesn't break after we give it to them, so their part shouldn't break after they've given us."

chunks.heading: Running the team: hire only the best, decide by consensus
chunks.text:
- NeXT's policy team is eight people. They try to separate the roughly 25 really important decisions a year from the rest, and on those they talk until everyone agrees.
- His reasoning: if you tell someone to "buy into" a decision they disagree with, you end up paying them to do what they think is right while forcing them to do what they think is wrong, and "sooner or later it outs".
- "I don't view that we pay people to do things... What's harder is to find people to tell you what should be done." He pays people a lot to tell him what to do. He can't recall once saying "dammit I'm the CEO and we're doing it this way". He has told someone "you're off the team" only once or twice, after a prolonged divergence.
- Biggest change since Apple: a longer-term view of people. When he sees something done wrong, his instinct is still to fix it himself, but he now asks how to help the person learn, because "we're building a team here and we're gonna do great stuff for the next decade, not just the next year".
- On hiring, he won't compromise. Recent hires include a VP of Marketing who spent seven or eight years at Microsoft (Mike Slade), a CFO from Intel (Marcel Ghani) and a COO he chased for about a year and a half (Peter van Cuylenburg). Great people take a year or more to pry loose. After meeting someone truly good, he says, everyone else is second best, so "I've always found it best not to compromise and just keep chipping away."

chunks.heading: Technology windows and why consultants learn only a fraction
chunks.text:
- A "technology window" opens when several technologies from diverse places come together to make a quantum leap possible. In his experience it takes about five years to build a commercial product that exploits the window, and about another five years to exploit it in the market.
- Examples: the Apple II lasted 15 years, DOS has lasted over ten, and the Mac is eight years old and has four or five more. They last "because they're really hot", not out of convenience.
- NeXT's first product failed: the cube sold only 10,000 units, because they "weren't quite there yet". The Mac was a course correction off the Lisa, which cost about $100 million. He says the window has opened after six years, and NeXT now has about five years of work to exploit it.
- He calls object-oriented technology the biggest technical breakthrough since graphical user interfaces in the early 80s, possibly bigger.
- On consulting: without owning something for years, taking responsibility for recommendations and "accumulating scar tissue" from mistakes, one learns only a fraction. He compares it to a two-dimensional picture of a banana, which you can show your friends but never taste. Consultants are also a variable expense, and in hard times "you find yourself variable".
- On higher education, he says discount heavily and sell there. It gives the best feedback and trains bright people you or your customers hire later. NeXT sold on about 350 US campuses and was the top-selling workstation there. Research projects like Athena rarely become products, because pioneering ideas and commercializing them take different people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1994 interview, Jobs explains how Apple grew out of Silicon Valley's values, blue boxes and the Homebrew Club. He argues for acting young with nothing to lose, building for yourself, asking boldly, and learning that the world can be changed.

chunks.heading: Starting Apple young, with nothing to lose
chunks.text:
- Steve says to start a company young: "we have absolutely nothing to lose." At 20 he had no family, no children, no house, and a Volkswagen van.
- His reasoning: even if they crashed and burned, "the experience will have been worth 10 times the cost," so there was no risk.
- He argues the only thing you really have in life is time, and investing it in great experiences means "you can't possibly lose."
- You can go to college and become a lawyer at 25, and nothing stops you. Older founders can succeed, but it is easier before you carry responsibilities to other people.
- Advice: "don't wait. Do something when you're young."

chunks.heading: Building what you yourself want
chunks.text:
- Apple was a classic Silicon Valley startup in two ways. Steve and Wozniak both had ties to Hewlett-Packard, which modeled how to build a company on values, not just profit.
- He admires the HP way. Its first value was making a profit so the company could continue, followed by how to treat individuals. He calls it "very idealistic" and says it influenced Apple.
- Apple built a product its founders wanted themselves. They knew exactly what they wanted in a computer, so they could do the marketing as well as the engineering.
- The same pattern started HP, which made test equipment for engineers.
- This changed later, once Apple sold to people unlike its founders. In the first several years, customers were "just like us."

chunks.heading: Blue boxes and the power of ideas
chunks.text:
- At 12, Steve phoned Bill Hewlett, who was listed in the Palo Alto phone book. He asked for spare parts to build a frequency counter. Hewlett gave him the parts and a summer job on the HP assembly line.
- He and Wozniak built blue boxes, devices that emit the tones the phone network used to signal between its computers. They fooled the network into opening up free calls anywhere in the world.
- Theirs was the first digital blue box in the world, built for about $100 of parts. It took roughly six months of discovery to work out. The boxes were illegal, which he notes.
- The lesson: two teenagers could control hundreds of billions of dollars of infrastructure from Los Altos and Cupertino. That taught him "the power of ideas."
- He says if they hadn't made blue boxes, "there would have been no Apple." It gave them the confidence that they could build something and make it work, and a sense of magic that they could influence the world.

chunks.heading: Watch the fringe, not the mainstream
chunks.text:
- His rule for predicting the next five years: "you don't look in the mainstream, you look at the fringe."
- In 1975 the fringe was the Homebrew Computer Club. Its members built their own computers because mainframes cost $50,000 to $100,000.
- The club met every two weeks at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center on Wednesday nights. He called it the most important day of his life, and he spent his spare time preparing for it.
- Despite being shy, he set up his computer with a Sears color TV and answered questions at the demo period. They went when it was 30 to 40 people; it grew to 200 to 300.

chunks.heading: Asking, acting, and willingness to fail
chunks.text:
- Venture capitalists turned them down, and one called Steve "a renegade from the human race" because of his long hair. He says "thank god," because those investors would have ended up owning most of the company.
- He argues Apple showed that great ideas are not the exclusive province of people with gray hair.
- On asking: "I've never found anyone who said no or hung up the phone when I called. I just asked."
- "Most people never pick up the phone and call. Most people never ask." He says that separates people who do things from people who dream about them.
- "If you're afraid of failing, you won't get very far." You have to be willing to crash and burn, whether on a phone call or in starting a company.
- He tries to be responsive when people ask him, to pay back that debt of gratitude.

chunks.heading: Iterating from the Apple I to the Apple II, and finding marketing help
chunks.text:
- The Apple I sold about 200 units. He says it was "50% right" and taught them how to make the next big jump, and they learned from the market what people wanted.
- That learning made the Apple II a giant success. It launched in April 1977 at the West Coast Computer Faire and sold maybe 10 million units over its life. He calls it the first really successful personal computer "by a mile."
- That fall he realized they needed advertising. An Intel ad in a technical journal caught his eye, so he called Intel to ask who made it.
- The answer was Regis McKenna. Regis nearly kicked them out at first but took them on as a client.

chunks.heading: Computers as a countercultural cause
chunks.text:
- Steve describes the personal computer industry as a countercultural movement out of the 1960s. It stood for the individual against the big-brother world of centralized mainframes.
- Apple's colorful logo set it apart from IBM's stark black and white one. Everything before the PC was big, massive, and centrally controlled.
- Startups of that kind were staffed by youngsters with little structure, but with a process everyone understood: get something done and make a difference.
- "Give something back" was a phrase he kept using. It was a sense of being part of a cause or crusade, not just a company.

chunks.heading: Work is sediment, and life can be changed
chunks.text:
- He expects all his work to be obsolete by the time he's 50. The Apple II is obsolete, the Apple I was obsolete years ago, and the Macintosh is nearing obsolescence.
- His analogy: this field doesn't produce a Principia that lasts 200 years or a painting admired for centuries. He compares it to sedimentary rock: you add a layer to the mountain, and only a rare geologist sees it.
- His closing advice: when you grow up you're told "the world is the way it is" and to avoid bashing into the walls. That is a very limited life.
- "Everything around you that you call life was made up by people that were no smarter than you. And you can change it. You can influence it."
- Once you learn you can poke life and something pops out the other side, you can mold it. "Once you learn that, you'll never be the same again."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jobs explains that great products optimize for one job and accept the second will be sub-optimal. He demos podcasting and Spotlight (built into the OS so it works better), describes how Pixar edits stories before animating, and says Apple avoids markets controlled by gatekeepers like carriers and cable companies.

chunks.heading: Competition, constraints, and why the iPod stays narrow
chunks.text:
Steve argues that products fight opposing constraints, and you must optimize for one job.
- Example: the PlayStation Portable is a great game machine but a poor music player, mainly because "it doesn't fit in your pocket."
- Games want big screens; music players want to fit in a pocket. "You have to pick one and optimize for it," and the second thing you do will be sub-optimal.
- On video: headphones give the same experience as great speakers, but "there's no such thing as headphones for video," so a small device can't match a 50-inch plasma at home.
- On wireless in an iPod: 802.11 drains battery. The deeper issue is that browsing and buying music is better on a computer with a big screen, where you can see many things at once. Steve calls this "one of the geniuses of the iPod."
- He holds that the iPod's market share rose over the prior year, and says Apple's focus is simply on "putting out the best products."

chunks.heading: Why Apple avoids phones and carrier-controlled markets
chunks.text:
Steve explains that Apple's strengths do not fit industries run by gatekeepers.
- Apple's greatest successes have not been in the Fortune 500, because it is not good at "going through orifices" (corporate buyers, carriers) to reach end users.
- If Apple can't succeed with 500 corporate gatekeepers, he asks how it would succeed with the four US carriers.
- Carriers have gained the upper hand and hand handset makers "big thick books" dictating what the phone will be; "that's not the way you work."
- Carriers add 3G, video and music to raise ARPU, but it isn't rising (camera phones didn't drive photo sending). Selling songs at $2-3 on phones would be a lousy buying experience costing 2-3x a computer purchase.
- On the Motorola deal: initially just an iTunes player on some phones, with music transferred from a PC or Mac, not a store interface.
- He rejected an MVNO as an answer, saying it's unclear such ventures endure as an industry gets more competitive.
- On the claim that phones will absorb the iPod, he declined to answer directly and left it to "our actions in the future."

chunks.heading: Subscriptions, record labels and pricing
chunks.text:
Steve says Apple is "not religious" about subscription music and asks customers what they want.
- Few customers ask for subscriptions. Three possibilities: not enough want them, enough want them, or people want a discovery layer on top of purchases.
- Yahoo's $5/month annual price was "substantially below their costs"; he predicted prices would rise as they gain customers. Apple staff had a betting pool on how soon (his guess: 5 months).
- Labels love subscriptions because they can keep raising prices, as cable did. Customers fear music disappearing when they stop paying and don't know future rent. A guaranteed $5/month for 10 years might be more compelling.
- Apple does ask customers: "we're out talking to iTunes customers constantly and non-iTunes customers constantly." Not driven by surveys, but uses them to course correct.
- Label economics on iTunes: labels earn more per song than on CDs because no marketing and no returns.
- Scale: over 400 million songs sold, over half a billion a year pace, over 70% share of legal downloads, which is still only about 5% of music distributed on CDs.
- Labels keep pushing to raise prices. Apple resisted. Apple also declined to fully back the industry's "intent" standard in the Grokster case because an engineer's intent could make Apple liable.

chunks.heading: Podcasting in iTunes 4.9
chunks.text:
Steve previewed podcast support, due within roughly 60 days, on Mac and Windows.
- Podcasting is "iPod and broadcasting"; it began as "Wayne's World for radio." Anyone can publish a show and listeners subscribe, with new episodes landing in iTunes and syncing to the iPod.
- Stats cited: 29% of US iPod users had listened to a podcast (Pew survey), over 8,000 podcasts, 6.2 million Google entries. No FCC regulation since it uses the internet, not spectrum.
- Until now it required a clunky third-party app. Apple built subscribe and unsubscribe into one button, with a podcast directory in the music store.
- Everything is free; he expects an advertising-supported model "just like free radio."
- Content from KCRW, Clear Channel, Infinity, Sirius, NPR, BBC, Newsweek, Businessweek, Forbes, Washington Post, Disney and Adam Curry's Daily Source Code.
- Features: artwork that changes during a show, chapters, links to buy songs, and an explicit flag. Podcasts need not be hosted by Apple, any RSS feed can be added, and a submission service will be automated. Apple will highlight top podcasts with editorial, "just like we do with music."

chunks.heading: The Mac, the iPod halo effect, and Apple stores
chunks.text:
Steve credits the iPod with pulling people toward Macs.
- Mac growth was three to four times the industry's in recent quarters. He credits "that iPod halo" and the retail stores.
- Stores: 105 stores (100 in the US), over a million visitors per week. The Genius Bar offers free help; the New York store has close to 100 geniuses.
- Mac US share is "starting with a four now." He has "given up predicting" a 10% share.
- Philosophy: "make the best personal computers in the world," the best OS, and awesome apps. Customers "are in love with their products."
- On Mac OS X security: no known virus spreading in the wild. He said Avie Tevanian insisted on requiring name and password authentication to load apps, which Steve's team resisted for a year before conceding. He warns never to be cavalier about security and doesn't market it, since it's a "red cape on the bull."
- Apple doesn't proactively push into corporations, but "hardly ever says no" when they want Macs.
- Xbox team at Microsoft bought roughly 4,000 Macs for development.
- On subnotebooks (no optical drive, about 15% of the notebook market), he admitted Apple had its hands full with the other 85% and that "maybe we should take another look."

chunks.heading: Tiger, Spotlight and Dashboard
chunks.text:
Steve explains Tiger as Apple's best OS release by acclaim and sales.
- Spotlight: finding things on a computer had become harder than searching the whole internet. Apple built search into the OS instead of an add-on.
- Three advantages over Google/Microsoft/Yahoo desktop search: far more comprehensive (apps, preferences, PDFs); the OS tells it when files change so results are never stale; and apps (Microsoft is building it into Office) can adopt it.
- Design reasoning: users hit a vertical learning curve at the file system. Email, iTunes and iPhoto already manage files in apps. Spotlight is the last step, so he expects consumers to use the Finder less, with file management becoming "an app for pros."
- On previews, he said people mostly find items by name and type, and conceded Apple "should go look at" richer previews.
- Dashboard: hit one key and widgets (clocks, weather, stocks, flight tracker, calculators) appear instantly and vanish just as fast. Third-party widgets include Amazon, CNN, and a countdown. He called it likely "the most popular feature of Tiger."

chunks.heading: Pixar: story first, edit before you make it
chunks.text:
Steve describes how animation differs from live action and why Pixar wins.
- Live action shoots 10-100x more footage than ends up on screen and builds the film in the editing room, when it's too late to fix problems. Animation is too expensive for that.
- Walt Disney's solution, which Pixar still follows: "edit our film before we make it, not after." Storyboards, filmed, with scratch voices and music, then iterated thousands of times in reels. Only when it works do they animate.
- "The story is king" is often said but abandoned under production pressure. Pixar has a story crisis on every film and stops production to fix the story. John Lasseter's saying: "no amount of technology will turn a bad story into a good story."
- Tech: about 120,000 frames per movie. Early frames took about 3 hours to render, and today's take about 3 hours even with computers roughly 10,000x faster, because "the appetite grows just as fast." The Incredibles is far richer than Toy Story, and Cars goes further. Pixar uses Macs and Linux PCs.
- Movies aren't zero-sum like computers: good movies help each other. He expects Pixar will someday have a movie that underperforms.
- On piracy: content will always reach the internet ("all there needs to be is one hacker"). The answer is business models "more enticing than free off the internet." Movies are already easy and cheap to watch, unlike CDs at $16.

chunks.heading: Trade secrets, leaks, and personal reflections
chunks.text:
Steve defends Apple's lawsuit against bloggers who published confidential Apple documents.
- His line: the law says journalists have First Amendment rights, "except if they break the law," and these people took trade secrets with Apple Confidential stamps and published them. He notes Intel and others filed briefs in support, and that courts have occasionally allowed publication for the public good, but this isn't one of those cases.
- He distinguishes serious editorial outlets such as the Wall Street Journal from a world where "anybody can be a journalist" without supervision.
- Apple employees may not blog about Apple, to protect secrets. Steve himself doesn't blog because it's time-consuming.
- He pulled Wiley books from Apple stores over how Apple was treated, saying "we just decided we didn't want to do business with them."
- On Windows Media Audio: Apple chose open-standard AAC over WMA, saying Microsoft's license terms were "so onerous" Apple shelved them.
- On his health: his pancreatic cancer was a rare curable form, treated by surgery. He learned about the body's recuperative ability and was moved by the well-wishes: "it had a few blessings in disguise."
- On TV: cable and phone companies subsidize set-top boxes, which distorts the market and limits innovation, making it hard for TiVo or Xbox to supplant the box.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jobs pitches NeXT's WebObjects at Internet World, arguing the web's "act two" is the server and dynamic page generation rather than static pages and browser tweaks. Demos for Dodge, Reebok and Sharper Image show the idea. Mostly product-specific, with a few durable points on free-to-premium pricing, speed of building, and letting software do repetitive work.

chunks.heading: Sharper Image, Reebok and Dodge: why dynamic pages beat static ones
chunks.text:
Steve frames the web in two acts. Act one was the browser and static publishing. Act two adds the server and dynamic services, which he says will be "the epicenter of the web act two".

- Most web pages are static: a human builds a page with a publishing tool, puts it on a server, and it never changes until a human changes it.
- Browser progress (plugins, Java, ActiveX) mostly expands the browser's UI toward Windows-level power. He calls that wonderful, and says Netscape and Microsoft will "duke it out" over it.
- His claim: the cool stuff has to happen on the server, "where you're responding to the user, doing tremendous amounts of processing" and building pages on the fly.
- He cites NeXT as a roughly $60 million, profitable, ten-year-old software company built on client-server enterprise software. Its enterprise know-how carried over to the web.

chunks.heading: Why pages must be built on the fly
chunks.text:
- Federal Express package tracking is his main example. The page showing where a package is did not exist before the package was sent, so the computer queries four mainframes and builds the page.
- That app took FedEx four months to build, and it is a very simple dynamic app.
- Search engines (WebCrawler, Lycos) build a page per query and are not hand-crafted for every search. The code behind them is "a lot of Perl code... it's not pretty".
- A catalog can have far too many permutations to build by hand. A customer might answer five questions and see only 10% of the catalog.
- If one change touches 3,000 pages, "the last thing you want to do is update 3,000 web pages by hand. You want the computer to do it."
- WebObjects layers on top of any HTTP server (Microsoft, Netscape, public domain). Page components such as pictures and text, held in databases or flat files, are stitched together with a scripting language, and pages are built on the fly.

chunks.heading: Dodge demo: speed of building
chunks.text:
- The Dodge site let a user filter by car, price range ($8,000 to $90,000) and model, then sort by model or price. Each choice rebuilt the page from a database.
- The user could drill into a Neon, pick the lime-green one, add option packages (package B and a subset package greyed out), and reach a ~$14,000 total.
- A leasing calculator took that price, a down payment and a 60-month term, and computed the amount.
- Steve says the app took two days to build, "and most of that time was the aesthetics". His contrast: the FedEx tracker took four months.
- His point: there are too many permutations to build by hand, so pages must be built from what the customer tells you about what they want, helping them "navigate through the morass of information".

chunks.heading: Reebok demo: guiding a customer to a decision
chunks.text:
- Planet Reebok aims to help people find cross-training shoes.
- The visitor picks a goal (lose weight, tone muscle, flexibility, overall fitness), self-rates cardio, strength and flexibility, and picks activities (bike, running, weights, yoga).
- The site returns matching shoes with match counts, sortable alphabetically, by price or by number of matches. The user adds shoes to a compare list and compares them.
- Steve says it was built in about a week by a few people, and that updating it by hand would mean changing 5,000 pages.
- He says it "looks a little different than the stuff you see on the web every day".

chunks.heading: Sharper Image demo: running a catalog without a staff of editors
chunks.text:
- A gift finder takes interests (gadgetry, fitness), price and demographic ("baby boomer") and builds a results page on the fly. Users can choose items per page and open a product page with several photos and ordering.
- Steve raises the operational problem himself. With static pages, 28 price changes in a day would need staff doing nothing but editing pages.
- He demos a web-based database administration app, built from the same components. He edits the massage chair record live, changing the layout, the price and the available colors (blue, red, yellow).
- On a fresh session the product page reflects the changes: a new layout, one picture, the new price, and a color pop-up.
- His takeaway: you need "much more robust tools" for dynamic applications, and "you cannot build applications like this with most of the tools out there today".
- Sharper Image's founder says the site went from first seeing the Dodge demo to live in weeks. He says he has never seen a company move that fast, and that typing in 400 products by hand took Josh a couple of hours each.
- He says Sharper Image spent about $35 million the prior year mailing its catalog to about 2 million people a month. He says the web could reach 10 or 40 million people a month at a far smaller fraction of the cost.
- Steve adds that NeXT gets paid partly in free stuff ("we're a company that likes stuff").

chunks.heading: Pricing and product strategy for WebObjects
chunks.text:
- Steve calls it a "radical pricing philosophy". Following the Netscape and now Microsoft model, NeXT gives away a surprisingly powerful base version and sells more powerful versions on top.
- Over 20,000 copies were downloaded from the website. This is server software, not client software. Roughly 12,000 of those downloads were for Windows NT, the most popular platform.
- The three tiers:
  - **Base (free):** a rich set of ready-made objects, including a virtual showroom app, but you cannot add your own.
  - **Pro:** lets you add your own objects, needing a compiled language because many clients hit them and they must run fast. It also talks to databases.
  - **Enterprise:** technology for enterprise-scale web apps and very sophisticated database access.
- Reason for giving away the base: "we think this should be essential on every web server. Every web server should be turbocharged."
- It works with every browser (it serves standard HTML) and every HTTP server, on NT, Solaris and NeXTSTEP.
- Language strategy: NeXT's own WebScript, plus JavaScript and Visual Basic as scripting languages. Compiled Java is planned for later in the year, "because we really believe in those languages and we want people to have a choice".
- Customers he names: Merrill Lynch (large internal then external apps), Motorola (intranets), Disney, DreamWorks (internal production management for the whole studio), Fannie Mae, Reebok and Sharper Image.
- His call to action is to download WebObjects free, layer it on your existing Netscape or Microsoft server, and build dynamic applications instead of static ones. He closes with "we're all just getting started" and that this is a new era of dynamic websites.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At the D1 conference in 2003, Jobs explains the personal computer as the "digital hub", demos the new iTunes Music Store, and says why Apple passes on tablets, PDAs and phones. He also covers how tech and content cultures misunderstand each other, and the hardest part of turning Apple around: laying people off.

chunks.heading: The digital hub strategy and why the PC stays at the center
chunks.text:
- Steve describes three ages of the personal computer: the hobbyist tool (Apple II, 1977, aimed at the many software hobbyists who had no soldering iron), the productivity age (kicked off by the first spreadsheet), and the internet age.
- He says Apple believes a third great age is coming, where the PC becomes "your digital hub" for photos, movies and music. Apple articulated this 3 years earlier, and "hardly anybody's delivered on it."
- Examples: a digital camera is useless without a PC, and anyone under 25 has their whole music library on a PC rather than on CDs.
- Why the PC stays the hub: it has a very big hard drive, display and keyboard, a fat pipe to the internet, and a processor that runs big applications.
- The iPod is a "satellite device." You couldn't run a music store on it because browsing needs more screen real estate, and a pocketable form factor fights a big screen "unless there's a breakthrough in foldable displays."

chunks.heading: Why Apple won't build a tablet or PDA
chunks.text:
- **Tablet:** Steve says Apple has no plans for one and thinks tablets will fail. Notebooks are already used for taking notes in meetings, so the real issue is handwriting versus keyboard.
- Apple has the best handwriting recognition technology in the world (after the Newton pain), "It doesn't matter. It's really slow to write stuff." Anyone with volume of email needs a keyboard.
- He jokes that people learned to type because "death would eventually take care of" the non-typers.
- He sees tablets as a niche: a third computer for rich people to read on.
- **PDA:** he estimates 90% of PDA users just want to get information out, and only 10% do major input. Cell phones will carry that data.
- Apple chose to put resources behind the iPod instead of a PDA. Its approach is to write great software that syncs the PC's data to the phone (the Palm cradle model), and to work with Nokia, Motorola and others.
- Why not make a phone: Apple isn't great at selling to the Fortune 500's 500 CIOs, and phones have only about five carriers to go through. "We'd rather run an ad for millions of people and let everybody make up their own mind."

chunks.heading: iPod focus: "It's the music, stupid"
chunks.text:
- Steve says the iPod had sold 700,000 as of a few months earlier, and he expects the millionth sometime later in the summer.
- Video and photos on the iPod are "speculative markets." Watching movies on a tiny screen "is really not very much fun," and the best portable movie device today is a PC with a DVD in it. Photos are better shown by plugging into a TV. Apple has such things in the lab.
- Music is a real, tangible market: "Music's been around for a long time... tens of thousands of years," and portable listening is already huge. Steve says to bring value to a proven market.

chunks.heading: How Apple missed MP3s, then caught up
chunks.text:
- Apple was near last to MP3s because it was focused on video. It had invented FireWire, licensed it, and everyone else shipped it in camcorders before Apple put it in the iMac.
- Chain: FireWire, then iMovie (editing "without reading a manual"), then the need to put the result somewhere, so Apple pioneered DVD-writing drives with Pioneer and wrote iDVD.
- Music "happened around the side," and Apple "got hit over the head with a brick."
- Catch-up: CD burners in almost every machine, iTunes ("some think is the best jukebox software in the world"), and the iPod in under a year.
- Apple is also the largest video editing supplier in the world, with Final Cut Pro well ahead of Avid in pro editing.
- The "Rip, Mix, Burn" ad: "rip" meant pulling the bits off a CD you own. Executives without teenagers read it as "rip off."

chunks.heading: Walking the middle path: iPod and the iTunes Music Store
chunks.text:
- Steve says Apple believes 80% of people stealing music would rather be legal if offered a compelling legal way.
- The iPod was built to avoid being a "theft shuttle." It syncs with only one iTunes library, so a friend's music can't be copied back. It is a compromise: "Both sides have to give up something to walk the middle path."
- He says nothing is unhackable, so the goal of DRM is to "keep honest people honest."
- Store features: buy, don't rent (people want to own music). The store is built into the iTunes jukebox rather than a web browser because browsers are slow and not interactive, and bought songs go straight into the library.
- Free 30-second high-quality preview of every song (about 20% of a track). One-click downloads, using the same idea as Apple's online store (between a billion and two billion dollars a year), which shares one-click with Amazon.
- Pricing: 99 cents a song ("three songs for the price of a Starbucks latte"), albums mostly $9.99 (range $7.99 to $11.99). Songs can be used on three Macs, any number of iPods and any number of CDs. Over 200,000 tracks, over 3 million sold in 4 weeks, with a Windows version coming by year end. The Beatles not yet available.
- Over half of tracks sold were bought as albums. Steve guesses labels will lower album prices over time.
- Long tail: labels' online catalogs can be much larger than the roughly 20% of a catalog that record stores stock, so "catalogs are going to be worth a lot."
- He also mentions browse by genre and artist as something not seen before online.

chunks.heading: Bridging tech and content cultures
chunks.text:
- Steve says he learned at Pixar that tech and content industries don't understand each other. Techies think creative work is guys on a couch drinking beer. In reality creative people are just as disciplined and work as hard. Hollywood thinks technology is something you write a check for and buy, not realizing it is created with passion.
- He calls bringing these cultures together one of Pixar's greatest achievements.
- Labels' key skill is picking which of 500 acts will be the next Sheryl Crow, which is intuitive with little data. So it wasn't surprising they missed Napster.
- Apple told them MusicNet and PressPlay would fail and was dismissed. About 9 months later labels called back.
- Argument that won them over: the real competitor was Kazaa, which offered unlimited burning, permanence after you stop paying, and portable players. Offering fewer rights is like "a big sign up that says Kazaa this way."
- Why labels trusted Apple: a smaller sandbox (about 10% of the market, so failure stays contained), control of the whole stack (OS, apps, computers, iPod), and a big company with money to sue.

chunks.heading: Competition, markets and hard decisions
chunks.text:
- On whether others will copy iTunes: Steve says it's harder than it looks. Getting label rights is hard, it takes real software work, and it needs a client app plus a jukebox. Apple would be open to supporting other portable players but few had asked.
- On speech: it's been "5 years away" for 30 years, like nuclear fusion; even 1% errors drive people nuts.
- Wi-Fi: Apple was first with low-cost Wi-Fi (AirPort), first to ship 802.11g (54 Mbps), and expects G to win over A because it's compatible with B. Networks will "just disappear."
- Market share by segment: consumer share more than doubled in a year to 5-10%. Creative pros have been depressed for years and Apple made mistakes in education. Retail: almost 60 stores, over 15 million visitors in 2 years, "the best buying experience for a personal computer on the planet."
- Advice on what he'd bet on at 17: biosciences, though he didn't foresee tech at that age.
- Hardest decision after returning to Apple in 1997: laying people off. Individual contributors were "unbelievable" ("we bleed six colors"), but management had to change. He did the cuts in the first year, while competitors laid off tens of thousands, and Apple decided to "innovate our way through this downturn" by shipping more products than ever.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jobs reports on his first four weeks back at a struggling Apple. He diagnoses a missing strategy, not missing talent, and calls for focus on where Apple is still relevant. He announces a new board and the Microsoft partnership, and ends with the "think different" idea of making tools for creative people.

chunks.heading: Steve's turnaround diagnosis of Apple (Macworld Boston, August 1997)
chunks.text:
After four weeks back, Steve reports that the popular claims about Apple were mostly wrong:
- "Apple's not as relevant as it used to be everywhere, but in some incredibly important market segments it's extraordinarily relevant."
- Apple is "executing wonderfully on many of the wrong things." The organization can execute, but the plan was wrong.
- He found no anarchy. He found people who "can't wait to fall into line behind a good strategy. There just hasn't been one."
- He sees a company with talented people who are still passionate about computing and need a great plan, then execution.
- The symptom is falling sales: $11.1 billion in 1995, $9.5 billion in 1996, and about $7 billion in the current year.
- His early steps: change the board first ("start at the top"), focus on relevance, invest in core assets, form meaningful partnerships (not just press releases), and define new product paradigms. He holds back product details for later in the year.

chunks.heading: Focus: find where you are still relevant and double down
chunks.text:
Steve identifies two segments where Apple still dominates and says it will focus on them.
- **Creative content** (publishing, design, pre-press): about 80 percent of computers in advertising and graphic arts are Macs. He cites 64 percent of internet websites as built on a Mac.
- He says Apple does a poor job here. Roughly 10 to 15 percent of Mac sales trace back to people using Adobe Photoshop as their power app, yet Apple and Adobe rarely co-market or work together on making a computer run Photoshop faster.
- **Education:** he asks who the largest education company in the world is and answers Apple. Of 100 Apple people he asked, only two had thought about it. Macs are 60 percent of computers in education and 64 percent of computers teachers use, a $2 to $2.5 billion annual business.
- Both markets grow over 20 percent a year. Apple's share has been slipping slowly, and he expects it to stabilize and turn around as Apple focuses.
- He calls the education figure "a bolt of lightning": an incredible base and legacy to build on.

chunks.heading: Core assets: the brand, the Mac OS, and the users
chunks.text:
Steve names Apple's core assets and says they were neglected.
- **The brand:** Nike, Coca-Cola, Disney and Apple belong on any list of the five greatest brands in the world. Apple "hasn't paid much attention to it in the last several years," and that will change.
- **The Mac OS:** "the best thing in the world," with 20 to 25 million active users, thousands of developers and a $1.5 billion software industry built around it. Steve says it has "yet to really be fully exploited."
- He rejects the belief that Apple is abandoning the Mac OS. It is a joke that the OS 8 release (code name Tempo) is followed by Allegro and then "Requiem": "it's absolutely crazy." Apple will do other things "because we're creative people, but at the core Apple is about the Mac OS."
- Mac OS 8 sold 1.2 million copies in two weeks, four times the forecast, and Apple was scrambling to ship.
- **The users:** "Apple's greatest core asset is you all." Steve admits Apple has not taken care of them. He called the support lines himself, "got very acquainted with the hold signal," and apologizes for the past.

chunks.heading: Rebuilding the board
chunks.text:
Steve announced the board change at the start of the turnaround.
- Two members stay: Ed Woolard (chairman and former CEO of DuPont) and Gareth Chang (president of Hughes International, bringing Asia experience).
- Four are added: Larry Ellison (Oracle, chosen partly for software industry expertise), Jerry York (former CFO of IBM and Chrysler, known for turnaround work), Bill Campbell (CEO of Intuit, formerly Apple's VP of sales and marketing and head of Claris), and Steve himself.
- The rest of the old board resigned. Steve thanks them as "very decent people" who tried to do the right thing, while saying that given Apple's situation it was time for a change and the directors agreed.
- No chairman is named until a new CEO is chosen.
- His criterion was deep industry expertise: "a lot of deep industry expertise who come together to say hey this world's a lot better place with a healthy Apple computer in it."

chunks.heading: Partnership with Microsoft: end the zero-sum mindset
chunks.text:
Steve announces a package deal with Microsoft, which began as a patent dispute settled professionally.
- A full patent cross license covers all existing patents and those filed in the next five years.
- Microsoft commits to release Office on the Mac for five years, matching the number of major releases on Windows, with the first targeted near year-end (it might slip into next year).
- Apple makes Internet Explorer the default Mac browser. Other browsers still ship and users can change the default: "we believe in choice."
- The companies collaborate on Java to keep their virtual machines compatible.
- Microsoft buys $150 million of non-voting Apple stock at market price and agrees not to sell it for at least three years.
- Steve's reasoning: "We have to let go of this notion that for Apple to win Microsoft has to lose." Apple must win by doing a really good job. If it fails, "it's not somebody else's fault, it's our fault."
- He adds that if Apple wants Office on the Mac, it should treat the company that makes it "with a little bit of gratitude."
- He says the era of framing this as Apple versus Microsoft "is over as far as I'm concerned." The goal is a healthy Apple making great contributions to the industry.
- He notes Apple plus Microsoft equals 100 percent of the desktop computer market, so each is the other's only other desktop player, which should drive more cooperation.

chunks.heading: "Think different": who Apple makes tools for
chunks.text:
Steve closes with the identity of the brand and its customers.
- You always had to "think different" to buy an Apple computer: the Apple II when computers filled giant rooms and had no software, the first computer arriving in a school, and the Mac as a computer that "used a totally different part of your brain" and was bought with an installed base of one.
- Today's Apple buyers are "the creative spirits in this world," people who are "not just out to get a job done, they're out to change the world." Apple makes tools for those people.
- He promises Apple will think differently too and serve the people buying its products since the beginning: "a lot of times people think they're crazy, but in that craziness we see genius, and those are the people we're making tools for."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1991 interview as NeXT CEO, Jobs argues that real progress comes from revolutionaries who leap beyond standards, not from incremental evolution. He says the industry is still in its infancy, and that companies must own their underlying technologies and be led by people who understand engineering and manufacturing.

chunks.heading: Where Steve says the 90s breakthrough will come from
chunks.text:
- Steve argues personal computing, mastered in the 80s, was about individual productivity and, at best, creativity. More than 50 million PCs shipped in the 80s on that promise.
- For the 90s he says improving individual productivity "isn't enough anymore." The real competitive advantage will come from group productivity and collaboration.
