- He calls this "interpersonal computing": using the same desktop tool that revolutionized analysis and planning (spreadsheets) and publishing (desktop publishing) to revolutionize human-to-human communication.
- He expects it to be the third revolution of the desktop computer in the first half of the 90s. He puts NeXT "about three or four years ahead" of tools like Lotus Notes. In his view Notes is okay but starts from a PC, "so you have a lot of inherent limitations."

chunks.heading: The industry splits into portable and powerful
chunks.text:
- Steve predicts the industry will bifurcate. Within two to three years, current-generation machines (IBM PCs, most Macintoshes) will all go portable and get smaller.
- Customers will also demand more power in three or four areas:
  - large color screens that can show photographs, as in high-end desktop publishing
  - motion video
  - very high-speed networking, at least Ethernet speeds
  - rich media moving around the network
- He says this second class of machine cannot be made portable. The next generation will be powerful, networked, color desktop machines.
- He describes NeXT's machines as "somewhere between a workstation and a personal computer," a description the interviewer offered and he did not dispute.

chunks.heading: Standards versus innovation: the evolution/revolution tension
chunks.text:
- Steve sees a constant, healthy tension in the industry between standards and innovation.
- Standards give everybody a baseline and a low-cost economic vehicle. But standard bearers "don't have any incentive to move forward and ultimately customers lose."
- Innovators use as many standards as they can, then leap up from them. This carries risk because they are outside the standard, but some succeed wildly.
- He calls Macintosh "a real revolution versus just an evolution." Most of the PC world has been evolutionary: the 286, 386 and 486.
- The revolutionaries that reach critical mass before the evolutionary players catch up survive and prosper. The rest get absorbed into the evolutionary path.
- Example: the IBM PC world finally got a graphical user interface seven years after the 1984 Macintosh.

chunks.heading: Why Steve expects a stagnant five years from Apple and IBM
chunks.text:
- He sees a lot more status quo than real revolution coming in the next five years.
- He expects little from the Apple-IBM relationship. He predicts "more of the same" from Apple (System 7, 8, 9) and from IBM (286s to 386s to 486s to 586s). Spreadsheets will "run a little faster but nothing really different."
- He says it will fall to companies like NeXT and others to provide the revolution. The standard bearers can catch up five, six or seven years later, as the PC world did with Macintosh.
- On Apple's strategy, he says the premise of Apple's existence is better, highly differentiated products that third-party developers can build exciting new applications on. If Apple gives that away by giving away its future system software, he is "not sure that the market needs Apple."

chunks.heading: Compound documents are a user interface problem
chunks.text:
- Steve pushes back on the claim that Xerox Star solved this. Star opened separate applications, and all of its applications were written by Xerox.
- It is easy to give a great demo when one company writes every app, because each app can know about every other.
- The real key is an underlying structure that lets third parties who never talk to each other have these capabilities within their apps. Nobody had yet done that well.
- He says the underlying technology is "very easy to hack up and give a demo of." The hard part is the user interface:
  - A spreadsheet brings its own paraphernalia, such as a formula bar and buttons.
  - A drawing program brings a palette, sometimes glued onto the document.
  - Nobody had figured out how to handle those context switches as the user moves between objects in a document.
- He judged GO's attempt too simple and not robust enough for real-life use, and said "you'll see some things next year" from NeXT.

chunks.heading: Early conviction and the PC's timeline
chunks.text:
- Steve corrects the "10th anniversary of the PC" framing:
  - The first modern PC was the Apple II in 1977, which sold five or six million units before being retired.
  - 1981 was the 10th anniversary of nothing; it was IBM's entry, which had a large effect, but the course was already plotted.
- By 1979 Apple was already shipping more computers by unit volume than IBM, which was then shipping big mainframes and a few minicomputers. He says that made them realize it would have a staggering effect.
- He started Apple at 20 and was 36 at the interview, roughly 16 years of building personal computers. He says his vocation, avocations and growing up are all the same thing and hard to separate.

chunks.heading: Why the industry is not mature
chunks.text:
- Steve rejects the view that the industry is mature and headed for rapid consolidation and a predictable few survivors.
- He says "we're about one inch down a road that's many miles long." Every major technological innovation creates opportunity for new players and a reorganization of the industry.
- He sees as much opportunity for innovation in the next five years as in any five-year period he has seen, and expects customers to get much better computers than today.
- He says he works with people who work very hard so the rate of innovation doesn't slow, and he wants most of it to keep coming out of the United States.

chunks.heading: Owning component technology: the US versus Japan
chunks.text:
- Steve says even though most computers are assembled in the US, a large share of the dollars for the components flows overseas.
  - The most expensive part is often the display (color CRT or flat panel). Almost all of those dollars go to Japan.
  - The second most expensive is dynamic memory (DRAM). Most of those dollars also go to Japan.
  - The third is hard disk drives. Most of those dollars go to US companies, even though the drives are mostly built in Singapore.
- He wants the most expensive components managed back to America. He says this takes real effort, especially in displays and DRAM, because factories cost half a billion to a billion dollars each and the engineering isn't built overnight.
- He warns against being "hollowed out" as an industry, where only final assembly, printing manuals and "the bow on the shipping carton" happen in the US.
- He rejects the argument that Wall Street short-termism is the cause:
  - A factory is an asset on the balance sheet, depreciated over many years, so building one doesn't hit the earnings statement.
  - Apple, IBM and others have hundreds of millions to billions in cash, so raising capital is not the problem.
- He locates the real problem in management: leaders without engineering or manufacturing backgrounds who don't appreciate their dependence on underlying component technologies. In Japan, he notes, the people running these companies are engineers or from manufacturing.
- His principle: "we have to have more accountability for our raw technologies and not just assume that we can be the final packager at the end." Component suppliers don't need the final packager and can go directly to the consumer, as Sony already has relationships to do.
- He claims NeXT has the most state-of-the-art factory in the whole industry.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At D8, Jobs explains how a resource-limited Apple succeeds by betting on rising technologies and dropping dying ones (floppy, serial ports, Flash). He also covers customer-first motivation over market cap, privacy as plain-English consent, and why TV innovation is blocked by go-to-market, not technology.

chunks.heading: Killing technologies early: Steve's "horses to ride" test
chunks.text:
- Apple isn't the company with the most resources, so it succeeds "by choosing what horses to ride really carefully, technically."
- Steve looks for technical vectors that have a future. Technologies go through "springs and summers and autumns" before the "graveyard of technology," and Apple tries to pick ones in spring.
- Choosing wisely saves enormous work and lets the team pour energy into making emerging technologies great on its platform, instead of spreading too thin.
- Apple's track record of cutting early:
  - Moved from the 5.25-inch floppy to the 3.5-inch floppy with the Mac (Sony invented it; Apple put it in the first products and made it popular).
  - Dropped the floppy entirely with the first iMac in 1998.
  - Dropped serial and parallel ports and was first to adopt USB, even though Intel invented it.
  - Was one of the first to drop optical drives, with the MacBook Air.
- People called Apple "crazy" for removing the floppy drive on the original iMac. Steve's answer: "sometimes you just have to pick the things that look like they're going to be the right horses to ride going forward."

chunks.heading: Why the iPhone and iPad skip Flash
chunks.text:
- Steve calls Flash a technology "that had its day but is really on... waning," while HTML5 is "on the ascendancy."
- Technical objections he cites: a lot of work to incorporate, battery life, and security. No smartphone was shipping with Flash at the time.
- Evidence the shift was real: an "avalanche" of sites moving to HTML5 video, which "looks better and works better and you don't need a plug-in." About 75% of web video was in Flash, with 25% heading toward 50% in HTML5.
- Consumers outside the industry were mostly unaffected, he says, apart from "holes" where ads sit, and those were closing fast.
- On developers, he points to over 200,000 apps on the App Store as proof the platform attracts developers.
- Sequence of events: Apple told Adobe to come back and show Flash running fast on the iPhone, and Adobe never did. The iPhone shipped without Flash. Adobe only "raised a stink" after the iPad shipped without it, and kept criticizing Apple in the press for months.
- Apple stayed professional and silent until it wrote "Thoughts on Flash," explaining its technical reasons. He says they were "just as true today as... 6 months or a year before."
- He insists "we weren't trying to have a fight," and says Apple likes Adobe and shares many Creative Suite customers.

chunks.heading: Product choices: what to emphasize, what to leave out
chunks.text:
- Steve's framing: products are "packages of emphasis." Some things are emphasized, some done less well, and some are chosen not to be done at all. Different people make different choices.
- On critics who call the iPad crippled without Flash: "if the market tells us we're making the wrong choices, we listen to the market."
- Apple has "the courage of our convictions" to leave out what it doesn't think makes a great product, and will "take the heat" because "we want to make the best product in the world for customers."
- Customers "are paying us to make those choices." If Apple succeeds they'll buy, and if not they won't. It "all works itself out."
- Proof point he offers: an iPad sold "every 3 seconds since we launched it."

chunks.heading: What keeps Apple's mission constant as it grows
chunks.text:
- Surpassing Microsoft in market value felt "surreal," but "it doesn't matter very much... It's not what makes you come to work in the morning. It's not why any of our customers buy our products."
- He wants Apple to "just remember what we're doing and why we're doing it."
- The motivation hasn't changed in 10 years: "there's nothing that makes my day more than getting an email from some random person in the universe who just bought an iPad over in the UK and tells me the story about how it's the coolest product they've ever brought home." That kept him going 5 years ago and 10 years ago "when the doors were almost closed."
- On the return to Apple: it was "about 90 days away from going bankrupt," and "much worse than I thought." He expected the good people to have left, but found "miraculous people."
- Asked why they stayed, many said "I bleed in six colors" (the old six-color logo), which he reads as "code for... I love what this place stands for." That made everyone work harder to make the company and its values survive.

chunks.heading: Doing the thing in the platform: why Apple built iAd
chunks.text:
- Insight from data: on phones, people spend their time in apps, not searching. They go to Yelp or a flight-status app rather than a search engine. Steve thinks this is because there was never "one place with 200,000 apps" where many are free and the rest very cheap.
- Purpose: "We're going into the ad business because we want to help our developers make some money so that they can keep providing free or really low-cost apps to customers." He says Apple won't make much money from it.
- Problem with existing mobile ads: tapping a banner throws you out to a web page, you can't easily get back to the exact place in the app, and in a game you won't make it back to the same spot.
- iAd's design: the ad takes over the screen with an interactive experience that "combin[es] the emotion of television with video," and a button returns you right where you left off.
- Why Apple does it: it owns the OS and can build it "in the bowels of the system," so a developer can add interactive ads with about 30 minutes of work, rather than custom work with each advertiser. Others could have done it, "but they weren't, so we did."

chunks.heading: Privacy: "plain English and repeatedly"
chunks.text:
- Steve says Silicon Valley isn't monolithic and Apple has "always had a very different view of privacy," taking it "extremely seriously."
- Example: location data. Apple worries a 14-year-old could get stalked because of a phone. Instead of relying on apps to follow a rule, the system itself shows a panel ("this app wants to use your location data. Is that okay with you?") every time an app asks.
- The curated App Store lets Apple reject apps that "want to take a lot of your personal data and suck it up into the cloud." He admits many in the Valley find this old-fashioned.
- His definition: "Privacy means people know what they're signing up for, in plain English, and repeatedly."
- Philosophy: "I'm an optimist. I believe people are smart and some people want to share more data than other people do. Ask them. Ask them every time. Make them tell you to stop asking them if they get tired of you asking them."
- Analytics rule: Apple restricted third-party analytics (the Flurry case) because developers' software was sending device and geolocation data to an outside firm without asking customers, which "violat[ed] every rule in our privacy policy." Analytics solely for advertising stay allowed, and he says Apple would talk to analytics firms later, "after we calm down."

chunks.heading: Content owners should know their customers
chunks.text:
- Steve's advice to Hollywood: technology offers "huge" opportunities for content owners.
- Marketing is shifting from expensive TV trailers to the web: Facebook, targeting, and direct communication with loyalty groups. It is becoming "more precise, cheaper, efficient."
- Lesson from music: record labels thought Best Buy and Target (or Tower Records) were their customer. "Their customer is the listener." What changed in music was the front end (distribution and marketing), not the back end of finding and developing artists, which "is just as important now as it ever was."
- The same will happen in film and TV: "The content is going to be just as valuable if not more valuable in the future."
- What studios should do: embrace the new front end, start knowing who their customers are, build ways to communicate with them, tell them when new product is out, and "let them watch it wherever they want, whenever they want."
- He expects this to move quickly in TV (some shows are free or sold the day after broadcast) and predicts big changes within about 24 months.
- On copy protection: content owners don't want a Napster repeat and "they're not in the business of copy protection, they're in the business of content creation." Apple sets no such rules itself. If it wants to sell their content, it follows their rules, tries to persuade them, and otherwise faces a simple choice.

chunks.heading: Why TV is stuck: the go-to-market problem
chunks.text:
- Steve's diagnosis: the TV industry's subsidized set-top box model (free or about $10 a month) "squashes any opportunity for innovation" because nobody will buy a set-top box. He cites TiVo, ReplayTV, Roku, Vudu, Sony, Apple, and a coming Google attempt.
- The result is a table full of remotes and boxes with different UIs. Fixing it would mean tearing up the set-top box and redesigning it "from scratch with a consistent UI across all these different functions," delivered in a way consumers will pay for.
- It isn't a problem of technology or vision; "it's a fundamental go-to-market problem."
- Why the phone worked: Apple partnered with carriers, but there's no national cable operator and every country has different standards and approvals (he calls it "Balkanized").
- Apple chose between a better TV, a tablet, or a better phone. Phone and tablet won because they could actually reach market.
- Hence Apple TV is a "hobby." Without a viable go-to-market strategy, "you're just making another TiVo."

chunks.heading: On life and fragility
chunks.text: - Asked whether he'd add anything to his Stanford commencement speech: he'd "just turn up the volume on it because the last few years have reminded me that life is fragile."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In this 1985 Playboy interview, Jobs explains why the Mac team built the computer for themselves, why craft must run all the way through a product, and why big companies lose great people to middle management. He also owns up to the Lisa and Apple III failures and describes making technology radically easier to use.

chunks.heading: The Macintosh as the "telephone" of computing
chunks.text:
- Steve argues the first computers asked users to learn "strange incantations," like the telegraph's Morse code, which took about 40 hours to learn. The telephone won because people already knew how to talk.
- His example: WordStar's manual is 400 pages. "To write a novel, you have to read a novel." People will not learn "slash q-z" any more than Morse code.
- He calls Macintosh "the first 'telephone' of our industry." It lets you "sing" as the telephone did: print styles, drawing, and pictures add expression beyond plain words.
- The mouse rests on a familiar metaphor. To flag a spot on a shirt you don't give coordinates, you point. Apple's tests found pointing faster for cutting and pasting, so it is easier and more efficient.
- Users do not need to understand how the machine works, just as drivers don't need to know how an automatic transmission works.
- Business payoff: five-page memos compress to one page when a picture carries the key concept, with less paper and better communication.
- He wants to inject "that liberal-arts spirit into the very serious realm of business." He rejects the myth that fun people must turn dull at work.

chunks.heading: Why Mac broke compatibility, and why it was built for ourselves
chunks.text:
- Steve gives two reasons for not being IBM-compatible:
  - He expected IBM to "fold its umbrella" and crush the clone makers.
  - The product vision: make computers "into appliances" for tens of millions of people, which the existing IBM-generation technology could not do.
- Reaching mainstream users needed a technology "radically easier to use and more powerful at the same time." The early adopters who stay up all night learning a machine were already served by the Apple II and IBM PC. He said it "may be the last chance" for a clean break.
- He denies it was ego: "It wasn't that we had to express our manhood by being different." The technology could not be this good if it were compatible.
- Apple II and IBM PC are "rivers carved in the rock bed of a canyon," taking seven and four years to carve. Mac blasted a third channel through in under a year.
- On picking standards: insisting on one standard now is like demanding one for automobiles in 1920, which would have blocked automatic transmission, power steering and independent suspension. "The last thing we want to do is freeze technology."
- Pricing: launch prices are high because low volume costs more, and Apple cuts prices as soon as it can. "I'd love it if Macintosh cost $1000."

chunks.heading: Building for yourself, and craft all the way through
chunks.text:
- The Mac team "built it for ourselves. We were the group of people who were going to judge whether it was great or not. We weren't going to go out and do market research."
- He contrasts Mac with IBM's PCjr, which he says was designed from market research for a demographic segment, hoping to make money. "Those are different motivations."
- The carpenter analogy: a maker of a beautiful chest of drawers won't use plywood on the back, even though it faces the wall. "For you to sleep well at night, the aesthetic, the quality, has to be carried all the way through."
- Making an insanely great product "has a lot to do with the process of making the product, how you learn things and adopt new ideas and throw out old ideas." The people who made Mac were "sort of on the edge."
- Working on Mac was "the neatest experience of my life." Nobody on the team wanted to release it, as if it would stop being theirs. At the shareholders' meeting the audience gave a five-minute ovation and the Mac team, seated in the front rows, cried.
- On hype: "Good PR educates people; that's all it is. You can't con people in this business. The products speak for themselves."

chunks.heading: Lessons from Apple III and Lisa
chunks.text:
- Steve calls the cost of Apple III "infinite, incalculable." Apple recalled the first 14,000 units and the machine never took off. He says the company emerged "much stronger."
- On Lisa, he lists the failures:
  - Priced around ten grand.
  - "Fortune 500-itis": chasing huge corporations when Apple's roots were selling to people.
  - Shipped about six months late, with software that "didn't come together."
  - Selling through only about 150 dealers, "absolutely foolish."
  - IBM arriving strongly at the same time.
- He says the hired "marketing and management experts" knew things that were "almost detriments" in a new kind of business. Being 23 to 25 and inexperienced, hiring pros "seemed like a good thing to do."
- When Scotty decided Steve lacked the experience to run Lisa, it "hurt a lot." The people hired from Hewlett-Packard and elsewhere brought a larger-machine, corporate-sales view and did not share the original vision.
- His response was to take a small group and "go back to the garage" to design Macintosh. He took the best people at Apple, the same people who then came up with the Mac.
- Decision-making: he tried never to have one person make all decisions. In early days he deferred to more experienced people, who were often right. In some important cases, going his way would have done better.
- Stakes: "We had to pull the rabbit out of the hat with Macintosh." Apple had nearly doubled in 1983, from $583,000,000 to about $980,000,000, almost all from the Apple II. Without Mac it would have stayed near a billion a year. If Mac failed, "my vision of the whole industry would have been totally wrong."

chunks.heading: Why companies decay, and how Apple tries not to
chunks.text:
- Steve's diagnosis: companies growing into multibillion-dollar entities "lose their vision." They add layers of middle management, lose their feel and passion for products, and creative people must persuade five layers of management to do the right thing.
- Great people leave environments where individual accomplishment is discouraged, "and you end up with mediocrity."
- Apple "is an Ellis Island company," built on "refugees from other companies," bright individual contributors who were troublemakers elsewhere.
- Example: Edwin Land dropped out of Harvard, founded Polaroid, and "saw the intersection of art and science and business and built an organization to reflect that." Being pushed out of his own company was "one of the dumbest things I've ever heard of." He calls Land "a national treasure" who should be held up as a model.
- Polaroid and Xerox would have topped a list of exciting companies 10-15 years earlier and now would be on no one's list.
- The test for him and John Sculley: making Apple an incredibly great $10-20 billion company that keeps its spirit. He says there are no models for this growth, and the dollar goal itself is "meaningless."
- Apple attracts people who put in 18-hour days and "really want to get in a little over his head and make a little dent in the universe."
- On the sense of mission: "Very rarely do we get a chance to put something back into that pool" of what society has made. Everyone senses "something much bigger than any of us here."
- On staying fresh: "death is the most wonderful invention of life. It purges the system of these old models that are obsolete." The test for Apple is whether it will embrace two young people with the next thing or "explain it away."
- On age: people "get stuck" in grooves, like a record. Artists in their 30s or 40s who contribute something amazing are rare. The exceptions are the innately curious, "forever little kids in their awe of life."

chunks.heading: Competing with IBM and reading the market
chunks.text:
- Steve says it is coming down to Apple and IBM. If IBM wins, "we are going to enter sort of a computer Dark Ages for about 20 years." Once IBM controls a sector, "they almost always stop innovation."
- The Frito-Lay analogy: it services more than half a million accounts a week with about 10,000 people replacing stale chips, holds over 80 percent share, and doesn't have to innovate. It studies small rivals' new products for a year or two, then copies and supports them. IBM plays the same game: virtually zero mainframe innovation in 15 years, and the PC "fundamentally brought no new technology," only a repackaging of Apple II ideas.
- Apple's counter is to go fast enough that they can't keep up, and to build "motherhood" (service and support) into the computer itself. IBM's focus is service, support and security.
- On market segments: he wants the "Fortune 5,000,000," meaning the roughly 14,000,000 small businesses, approached bottom-up by treating them as collections of people and focusing on the small work group rather than wiring whole companies.
- Hardware innovation will be hard for newcomers because of scale. Imitators of $100-200 million will be "struggling for your life." Most new innovators will work on software.
- On other players: A.T.&T. has great research technology but must learn to commercialize it and do consumer marketing, which will take years. Radio Shack "tried to squeeze the computer into their model of retailing" and missed the boat. He dismisses sub-$500 computers as "a brochure" for buying an Apple II or Mac, because they either tease or frustrate.
- On Japan: they "reinvent" rather than copy, studying a product until they understand it better than its inventor. That works for slow-moving targets like stereos and cars but is hard when the definition of a PC keeps changing. He expects them to figure out a decent computer in four to five years.
- Manufacturing response: Apple spent $20,000,000 on the industry's most automated factory and writes it off in two years rather than seven, planning to throw it away at the end of 1985 and build a better one. "That's the only way we can learn fast enough."

chunks.heading: Where computers are going, and education
chunks.text:
- Steve calls the computer "the most incredible tool we've ever seen," a writing tool, communications center, calculator, planner, filer and artistic instrument by changing software. He says "people are basically tool users."
- Computers as appliances: the long-term home case is linking to a nationwide communications network, which he expects to be "as remarkable as the telephone." He compares speculation to Bell, who couldn't predict the telephone's uses.
- Software history he credits: programming languages on microprocessors, VisiCalc (first real business use), Lotus (spreadsheet plus graphics in one program), then Mac and Lisa technology. Word processing is the most universally needed application. He expects an educational "VisiCalc" but not within 24 months.
- Education: computers are "the first thing to come along since books that will sit there and interact with you endlessly, without judgment," and could restore a Socratic experience when paired with enlightened teachers.
- Apple's education push: the Apple Education Foundation gives millions in cash and equipment. Apple wanted six universities making large commitments of over 1,000 machines each and $2,000,000 each, and found 24, including the entire Ivy League. IBM countered with giveaways, but colleges saw the software investment would dwarf hardware and chose Macs.
- Next software step: computer as "guide or agent" rather than servant. It would anticipate needs and notice patterns. "Triggers" would let it monitor conditions, such as selling a stock past set limits or writing personalized letters to sales reps who beat quotas by 20 percent, then report afterward. He guessed about three years away.
- His long view: a book lets you read Aristotle directly, but you can't ask him a question. Computers could capture the underlying principles of a thinker's world view, as Pong captured gravity and angular momentum, so you could ask an Aristotle or Einstein or Land. That is "for the next generation."
- Warning: technical illiteracy in politics and underinvestment in education risk America becoming a "second-rate industrial nation."

chunks.heading: Money, focus, and living with success
chunks.text:
- Steve says the money is "hardly the most insightful or valuable thing that's happened to me." He lost $250,000,000 in a year when the stock fell and said he wouldn't let it ruin his life.
- He gives growth figures with pride, as "yardsticks": about $200,000 in 1976, roughly $7,000,000 in 1977, $17,000,000 in 1978, $47,000,000 in 1979, $117,000,000 in 1980, $335,000,000 in 1981, $583,000,000 in 1982, about $985,000,000 in 1983. The milestone he prizes is seeing kids using 15 Apple computers in a classroom in 1979.
- On wealth: it is a responsibility. He says leaving huge sums to children "will just ruin their lives," and the challenge is to reinvest it in the world. "To give away a dollar effectively is harder than to make a dollar," because philanthropy lacks a measurement system, so you can't fail and learn. He wants actions, not words, to speak first.
- His favorite things don't cost money. "The most precious resource we all have is time," and he pays a price in not having much of a personal life.
- On identity: "If you want to live your life in a creative way, as an artist, you have to not look back too much. You have to be willing to take whatever you've done and whoever you were and throw them away." At the core are values, and outside images of you make it harder to keep growing.
- "I'm still a student. I'm still in boot camp." He cites the Hindu saying that for the first 30 years you make your habits and for the next 30 your habits make you. He hopes his life and Apple's will "weave in and out of each other, like a tapestry."
- On grace: the challenge is "to grow obsolete gracefully," turning the reins over to a generation that can "stand on our shoulders and go much further."

chunks.heading: Early influences: Hewlett-Packard, Woz, Atari, and the garage
chunks.text:
- Steve's father, a machinist who could fix anything, gave him things to take apart, and teacher Imogene Hill ("one of the saints in my life") kindled his passion for learning in fourth grade.
- At about 12 he saw his first computer at Hewlett-Packard on a Tuesday night lecture. At 12 or 13 he called Bill Hewlett from the phone book for parts, chatted for 20 minutes, and got a summer job on the HP line.
- He met Wozniak at 13 (Woz about 18), the first person who knew more electronics than he did. They built blue boxes and pulled pranks. He credits California's culture of experimentation, Dylan, Eastern mysticism, and the intellectual flow at Reed.
- The Altair (1975, under $400 as a kit) made a computer you could own. He worked at Atari, employee number 40, and let Woz in at night, which led to Woz's terminal design.
- The Apple I: they raised $1300 by selling his VW bus and Woz's HP calculator. About 150 sold for roughly $95,000, a bare circuit board with no case, power supply or keyboard.
- The Apple II's breakthrough: a finished product, fully assembled with its own case and keyboard, so you could be a software hobbyist rather than a hardware hobbyist. He says the power supply and case were key, and that the Apple "wouldn't have happened without Woz and… without me." Woz is a brilliant designer who isn't great at turning things into products.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1995 Smithsonian oral history, Jobs explains why he obsessed over only hiring A players, how the Macintosh team amplified their values a million to one, and why technology and art are not separate. He also argues people matter more than computers in education, and that perseverance and passion separate successful entrepreneurs.

chunks.heading: Building products: craft, humanism, and hands-on learning
chunks.text:
- Steve credits his father Paul, a machinist with no high school diploma, for giving him his own workbench at about five or six and teaching him to build things, take them apart and put them back together.
- A neighbor, Larry Lang (an HP engineer and ham radio operator), taught him electronics. Steve says Larry used Heathkits, which came with detailed color-coded manuals and a theory of operation.
- Steve says Heathkits gave "the sense that one could build the things that one saw around oneself in the universe." Things stopped being mysteries and became "the results of human creation."
- He says exploration and learning give the confidence that seemingly very complex things can be understood.
- At Apple he was proudest of where "the technical and the humanistic came together." His example is publishing: typographic artistry combined with technical excellence let people use a computer without arcane commands. He says this happened on the Apple II, the Lisa and "big time" on the Macintosh.
- He sees little distinction between an artist and a top-calibre scientist or engineer. Both pursue the same goal: to "express something of what they perceive to be the truth around them so that others can benefit by it."
- He describes the artistry as having an insight into what one sees and putting things together in a way no one else has. In the 70s and 80s, he says, the best people in computers would otherwise have been poets, writers and musicians, because computing was "a new medium of expression for their creative talents."
- He says "people put a lot of love into these products."
- He frames the Macintosh as "collective works of art much like twentieth century physics": a core group of fewer than a hundred people, more than ten million Macs shipped, and hundreds of millions of copies by the whole industry. He calls this a million-to-one amplification of values.
- His image for leverage is that changing the course of a vector near its origin makes it radically different a few miles out.

chunks.heading: Hiring only A players and the cost of keeping the wrong people
chunks.text:
- Steve says one of the few things he can contribute individually is to "instill in the organization the goal of only having 'A' players."
- His reasoning is the range of talent in each field:
  - Taxi drivers: best versus worst is about two to one, fifteen minutes versus thirty minutes across Manhattan.
  - Cooks: maybe three to one.
  - His field: the best versus the worst is "about a hundred to one or more."
  - Software: a good versus a great person is twenty-five to fifty to one.
- He concludes it "really pays to go after the best people in the world," in everything he's done.
- He says that sometimes his job has been to get rid of people who didn't measure up. He tries to do it humanely, but it "has to be done and it is never fun." He calls it the hardest, most painful part of managing a company.
- He admits that at times he was "pretty hard about it" and gave people no choices.
- He accepts that the people he fired may hate him and that this comes with the world he chose to live in.
- On teams, he says "one person can't do anything anymore." You build a team and owe it integrity of work, and everyone tries to turn out their best.

chunks.heading: Why Apple lost its way: values, not growth
chunks.text:
- Steve says Apple grew from nothing to two billion dollars while he was there (a billion-dollar company when the Mac launched, Fortune 300-something when he left), and growth did not ruin it.
- He says "What ruined Apple was values." He blames John Sculley for bringing corrupt values to the top, which corrupted some executives, drove out incorruptible ones and brought in more corrupt ones. They paid themselves tens of millions of dollars and cared more about glory and wealth than about "making great computers for people to use."
- The original vision was to make the Mac an appliance and get it to as many people as possible. Instead they went for outlandish profits for about four years, which "cost them the future."
- He says they should have taken reasonable profits and gone for market share. By his estimate the Mac would have had a thirty-three percent share or more, against a single-digit and falling share in 1995.
- His diagnosis: no one running any part of Apple was there when the Macintosh was made, so no one knows how to create the next one. The Newton was the last attempt.
- He compares Apple at its best to Sony, "the place that made the coolest stuff."
- He predicts "The Macintosh will die in another few years" and that market share, once below a threshold, spirals down, especially once developers stop writing applications.
- Apple stood for taking on IBM, as in the 1984 ad: "your way is wrong... this is not what we want our kids to be learning," and "we are going to show you the right way to do it."
- He says Apple never knew how to sell to corporate America and its attempts were "bungled." Macs sold to people who bought on merit rather than company name, against the era's "You never get fired for buying IBM."

chunks.heading: The kids can't wait: putting a computer in every school
chunks.text:
- Steve's 1979 view was that if there were just one computer in every school, some kids would find it and it would change their lives. Only about 10% of schools had even one.
- Apple wanted to donate a computer to every school in America: about a hundred thousand schools, roughly ten thousand high schools and ninety thousand K through 8.
- The company couldn't afford it outright. An existing law gave an extra tax deduction for donating scientific instrumentation or computers to universities for education and research. Extending it to K-8 and removing the research requirement would cut the cost to about ten million dollars, instead of over a hundred million.
- With Rep. Pete Stark, Steve drafted the bill, called "the kids can't wait bill." Senator Danforth introduced it in the Senate. He refused to hire lobbyists and walked the halls of Congress himself for about two weeks, meeting about two-thirds of the House and over half of the Senate.
- It passed the House with the largest favorable majority of any tax bill in history. It then died in Carter's lame-duck session when Bob Dole refused to bring it to the floor.
- California then passed its own version, and Apple gave away ten thousand computers in the state. Software companies donated software and Apple trained teachers for free.
- Steve calls it one of his great experiences and one of his biggest regrets that it failed nationally.

chunks.heading: Education: people over technology, and vouchers
chunks.text:
- Steve says he believes in equal opportunity, not equal outcome, and equal opportunity "more than anything means a great education."
- He credits fourth-grade teacher Mrs. Hill with saving him. She bribed him back into learning with a math workbook, five dollars and a giant sucker, then got him camera-making kits. He ground his own lens. He says he learned more that year than any other and that without her and a few others he'd "absolutely have ended up in jail."
- Despite helping put more computers in more schools than anyone, he says computers are not the most important thing. The most important thing is "a person who incites your curiosity and feeds your curiosity."
- His reason: computers are reactive, not proactive. Children need a guide, not an assistant. A week playing with gravity and why things fall needs no computer.
- He supports a full voucher system. In his view the real customers of education are the parents, who stopped paying attention, which let a monopoly take over. He cites a bumper sticker about the phone monopoly, "We don't care. We don't have to," and compares IBM in its day.
- His numbers: a $20,000 car lasts about eight years (about $2,000 a year), while California spent about $4,400 per pupil per year in public school.
- He expects a $4,400 voucher to do three things:
  - Schools would market themselves like crazy.
  - New schools would start. Idealistic twenty-five-year-olds could start schools instead of Silicon Valley companies.
  - Quality would rise under competition. Many public schools would go broke, which he calls painful at first but less painful than the current system.
- He wants teachers good enough to earn $100,000 at his company. He blames unions for turning education into a bureaucracy rather than a meritocracy.
- He says he once thought technology was the solution to most of the world's problems and now says "it just ain't so." Problems that are human, organizational and political must be attacked at the root.
- On TV: the programming is bad because the majority of people want to "turn on a television and turn off their brain," which he calls more depressing than a conspiracy.

chunks.heading: Lessons from Xerox PARC and NeXT
chunks.text:
- In 1979 he visited Xerox PARC and saw three things working: graphical user interfaces, object-oriented computing (Smalltalk) and networking (Ethernet, with about two hundred Altos on a LAN doing email).
- He says the GUI was so incredible that it "blinded me to see the other two." It took years to rediscover objects and networking, which he later brought into NeXTStep.
- He remembers knowing within ten minutes of seeing the GUI that every computer would work that way someday: "It didn't require tremendous intellect. It was so clear." He says the same holds for objects: all software will eventually be written with object-oriented technology.
- NeXT's mistake was repeating the Apple formula of making the whole widget while the industry was changing. He says NeXT would be "either the last company to make it or the first to not make it" and turned out to be the first that didn't. He says they should have gone straight to being a software company.
- Details he cites for the NeXT machine: totally plug and play, workstation power, and fit and finish in operation. Soft power on and off prevented data loss. It was the first computer with built-in CD-quality sound.
- NeXTStep recorded its first profit in nine years, with fifty million dollars in software sold. He expects it could become a few-hundred-million-dollar software company within three or four years.

chunks.heading: Pixar, the Internet, and why new companies keep winning
chunks.text:
- Steve says George Lucas's Lucasfilm group built digital compositing to avoid the noise that accumulates when you copy film optically. Star Wars composited up to thirteen film elements per frame.
- When Lucas stopped funding the group, Steve bought it and incorporated it as Pixar. He says eight of the ten most important revolutions in high-end graphics of the last ten years came out of Pixar, including software behind Terminator and Jurassic Park.
- Pixar's vision was to tell stories: the first completely computer-synthetic animated feature, Toy Story, due out November 1995 as Disney's Christmas picture, with Tom Hanks and Tim Allen. He calls Pixar the first digital studio, combining art and technology, and says it was probably close to ten years ahead of anybody else.
- On the Internet and Web, he gives three reasons for excitement:
  - Computers are becoming communications devices.
  - A three-person company can look as good as IBM or the Gap, with direct distribution cutting out middlemen, a levelling of big and small and near and distant.
  - Microsoft doesn't own it and probably can't.
- He argues the government should keep funding the Internet as a public trust. He puts the cost at about fifty to seventy-five million dollars a year, and says it should stay free.
- He argues that new companies always get a chance because "human minds settle into fixed ways of looking at the world." Large companies also have poor communication paths from the bottom to the top, with IBM and the PC as his example.
- He says "death is the greatest invention of life" because it makes room for the young, who see the world without preconceptions.

chunks.heading: Perseverance, passion, and how to spend a life
chunks.text:
- When people say they want to be an entrepreneur but have no idea, he tells them to "go get a job as a busboy or something until you find something you're really passionate about because it's a lot of work."
- He is convinced about half of what separates successful entrepreneurs from unsuccessful ones is pure perseverance. It is "pretty much an eighteen hour day job, seven days a week for awhile."
- You need an idea, a problem or "a wrong that you want to right" that you're passionate about to have the perseverance.
- On responsibility, he says he doesn't think of it as an individual's duty beyond doing "really good stuff" and getting it out for others to build on: "the work speaks for itself."
- He quotes the advice to live each day as if it were your last. His view is that what you leave behind is "your kids, a few friends and your work."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a candid 1995 interview, Jobs explains why great products come from content-obsessed teams of A players, not process or ideas alone. He covers the rock tumbler metaphor for teams, why monopolies rot product sensibility, and why taste and a liberal arts background drive computing.

chunks.heading: Why Steve got into computers and what early projects taught him
chunks.text:
- Steve first used a time-sharing teletype terminal at NASA Ames at about age 10-11. Writing a BASIC or Fortran program and getting back the results he predicted was "an incredibly thrilling experience."
- At 12 he phoned Bill Hewlett to ask for parts for a frequency counter. Hewlett talked to him for about 20 minutes, gave him the parts, and gave him a summer job at HP. That shaped his picture of a company: HP brought out a cart of donuts and coffee every morning, and it was "clear that the company recognized that its true value was its employees."
- At HP's Palo Alto labs he saw the HP 9100, the first desktop computer: self-contained, with a small CRT, programmable in BASIC and APL. He loved it.
- He and Wozniak built "blue boxes" after finding an AT&T technical journal that explained the signaling tones. AT&T's flaw was putting its computer-to-computer signaling in the same band as the voice. Their box was all digital, with no adjustments, and took three weeks to build.
- His lesson from blue boxing: "we could build a little thing that could control a giant thing." He says "I don't think there would have ever been an Apple Computer had there not been blue boxing."

chunks.heading: How Apple started: terminal to Apple I to Apple II
chunks.text:
- Steve and Woz built a terminal because they could not afford one and wanted free time-sharing access. The Apple I was that terminal plus a microprocessor, and it was built for themselves out of scavenged parts.
- Each hand-built Apple I took 40 to 80 hours and kept breaking. Friends wanted them too, so they made a printed circuit board to cut the build time to a few hours. Steve sold his Volkswagen bus and Woz sold his calculator to pay for the board artwork.
- Paul Terrell's computer store (a bike shop in Mountain View) offered to buy 50 fully assembled units. They bought parts for 100 units on net-30 credit, built 50, sold them to the shop at twice the cost to build, and got paid in 29 days. They paid suppliers on day 30.
- They then faced what he calls a profit-realization crisis, with the profit sitting as 50 computers in the corner. That pushed them to think about distribution and to call computer stores across the country.
- For the Apple II, Steve's ambition was "the first real packaged personal computer" for the thousand software hobbyists for every hardware hobbyist, so you would not need to assemble anything.
- Venture capitalist Don Valentine passed on them but referred Mike Markkula, who had retired from Intel at about 30. When Markkula offered money, Steve told him "no, no, we don't want your money, we want you," and made him an equal partner.
- They tooled up the Apple II and announced it at the West Coast Computer Faire, where Steve (21 at the time) says they "stole the show" with a projection TV showing the graphics.

chunks.heading: Business is mostly folklore: ask why
chunks.text:
- Steve says that in business "nobody knows why they do what they do. Nobody thinks about things very deeply."
- Example: factory accounting used "standard cost" with a quarterly variance adjustment. After about six months of asking why, he found it existed because information systems were too poor to know the real cost, so people guessed and fixed the guess at quarter's end.
- For the Macintosh he built an automated factory that knew exactly what something cost "to the second."
- He calls much of business "folklore," things done because they were done yesterday. If you ask a lot of questions, think and work hard, "you can learn business pretty fast. It's not the hardest thing in the world."
- On money: he was worth over $1M at 23, over $10M at 24 and over $100M at 25, but "I never did it for the money." He sees money as useful for investing in ideas without short-term payback. What mattered was "the company, the people, the products we were making, what we were going to enable people to do." He never sold his stock.
- He thinks everyone should learn to program, because it teaches you how to think, "like going to law school." He views "computer science as a liberal art."

chunks.heading: Xerox PARC and why companies lose their product sense
chunks.text:
- Steve visited Xerox PARC in 1979 and was shown three things: object-oriented programming, networked computers (over 100 Altos with email) and the graphical user interface. He was so blinded by the GUI that he missed the other two.
- The PARC version was flawed and incomplete, but within about 10 minutes it was obvious that all computers would work this way someday.
- His explanation of why Xerox squandered it applies to monopolies like IBM and Xerox: when a company has a monopoly, a better product does not increase its success, so sales and marketing people become the ones who make the company more successful and get promoted. Product people "get driven out of the decision-making forums."
- The company then forgets "what it means to make great products." The people running it have "no conception of a good product versus a bad product," no sense of the craftsmanship needed, and little feeling for helping customers.
- PARC people called Xerox's executives "tonerheads," and Steve says Xerox could have been "the IBM of the nineties" or "the Microsoft of the nineties."
- Related lesson on IBM's PC: its first product was bad, but IBM gave many other companies a vested interest in its success, and that saved it.

chunks.heading: Process versus content, and why ideas are not products
chunks.text:
- At Apple, Steve found that people from HP did not grasp the GUI. They thought soft keys at the bottom of a screen were the coolest interface, and they said a mouse would take five years to engineer and cost $300. Steve went outside to David Kelley Design, and in 90 days they had a mouse that cost $15 to build and was very reliable.
- His diagnosis of larger companies: "people get confused that the process is the content." IBM "has the best process people in the world. They just forgot about the content."
- His view: "the best people are the ones that really understand the content. And they're a pain in the butt to manage, but you put up with it, because they're so great at the content. And that's what makes great products. It's not process, it's content."
- The Lisa failed because it drifted from Apple's roots. At $10,000 it was "cheap" to HP-style people but impossible for Apple's market, distribution channels and customers.
- Steve lost the fight to lead Lisa, then formed a small team to build the Macintosh. The Mac target was a roughly $1,000 product. They negotiated the 68000 chip at a fifth of Lisa's price by committing to higher volume, and it launched at $2,500.
- The Mac effort also reinvented the factory (he visited about 80 automated factories in Japan), distribution and marketing. He describes it as "the machine to build the machine."
- On John Sculley's "disease": "thinking that a really great idea is 90% of the work." Steve says there is "a tremendous amount of craftsmanship in between a great idea and a great product." Designing a product means keeping around 5,000 things in your head and fitting them together in new ways, because the idea changes as you learn the trade-offs of electrons, plastic, glass and factories. "That process is the magic."

chunks.heading: Building teams: A players, the rock tumbler and direct feedback
chunks.text:
- Rock tumbler metaphor: as a boy, an old neighbor put ordinary ugly rocks in a coffee can with liquid and grit, ran a motor overnight, and the rocks came out polished. Steve says a team is the same: talented people "bumping up against each other, having arguments, having fights sometimes, making some noise," and "they polish each other" and the ideas.
- Dynamic range: in most fields the best is at most about 2x the average (a taxi driver, a car, a CD player). In software the gap between average and best is "fifty to one, maybe a hundred to one."
- He built his success on "finding these truly gifted people and not settling for B and C players, but really going for the A players."
- Once you assemble about five A players, they enjoy working with each other, don't want B and C players, and "it becomes self-policing." They hire more A players, so "pockets of A players" propagate. The Mac team was all A players.
- The Mac team members say it was the hardest they ever worked and one of the most intense, cherished experiences of their lives, though "some of those things are not sustainable for some people."
- On telling someone their work is bad: "it usually means their work is shit," or sometimes that he is wrong. With really good people you don't have to baby egos, because "what really matters is the work." The most important thing is to point out clearly why their work is not good enough, without questioning your confidence in their ability, to get them back on track. Some people hated this, but the really good ones found it beneficial.
- He says he doesn't care about being right: "I just care about success," and he changes his mind within minutes when shown evidence. "What matters to me is that we do the right thing."

chunks.heading: Desktop publishing, the LaserWriter and a marketing blunder
chunks.text:
- Apple got the first Canon laser printer engine shipped in the US and had it hooked to a Lisa. Then Steve visited ex-Xerox PARC people who were better, and he talked them (Adobe) into being a software company rather than a hardware one.
- Within two to three weeks Apple cancelled its internal project (some people "wanted to kill me"), bought 19.9% of Adobe for financing and some control, designed the printer controller, and shipped the LaserWriter.
- Nobody else at the company wanted it, because everyone thought a $7,000 printer was crazy. They understood sharing it over AppleTalk intellectually but not viscerally, because the last expensive thing Apple sold was Lisa. Steve pushed it through anyway.
- When he left, Apple was the largest printer company in the world by revenue.
- His "largest marketing blunder": announcing the "Macintosh Office" in 1985 instead of focusing on desktop publishing alone. "We should have just focused on desktop publishing."

chunks.heading: Apple's decline, Microsoft and taste
chunks.text:
- On leaving Apple in 1985: "I hired the wrong guy." He says that when the industry slid into a recession in late 1984, Sculley, who "didn't know what to do," left a leadership vacuum, and Steve believes Sculley chose him as the scapegoat. He argues it was a problem of execution, not competing visions: Apple needed stronger leadership, to focus spending on the Mac, and to rein in the Apple II area. He offered to start a research division with a few million dollars a year and was refused.
- In 1995 he says "Apple is dying," on a "glide slope," because it had a ten-year lead and "stood still." By his account the Mac was only about 25% different than when he left, despite roughly $5 billion spent on R&D, and Microsoft's catch-up ended Apple's differentiation.
- On Microsoft: he credits it as strong opportunists who "just keep on coming" and says they used the IBM deal as a springboard. It wrote terrible Mac apps in 1984 but kept improving them until it dominated.
- Its problem: "they just have no taste. They have absolutely no taste." They don't originate ideas or bring culture into products. Proportionally spaced fonts "come from typesetting and beautiful books," and Microsoft would not have them without the Mac. Their products have "no spirit" and are "very pedestrian." He compares Microsoft to McDonald's, and adds that what saddens him is not their success but that their products don't show more insight and creativity.
- His view on how to raise the bar: "take the best, and spread it around to everybody," so people grow up with better things and understand their subtlety.

chunks.heading: Taste, the liberal arts and the bicycle for the mind
chunks.text:
- A Scientific American article on locomotion efficiency ranked the condor first and humans about a third of the way down, but a human on a bicycle beat the condor. This led to his idea that humans are tool builders and that "the personal computer is the bicycle of the mind." He believes the computer will rank at or near the top of human inventions.
- On how to know the right direction: "it comes down to taste. It comes down to trying to expose yourself to the best things that humans have done, and then try to bring those things into what you're doing."
- He quotes Picasso, "good artists copy, great artists steal," and says "we have always been shameless about stealing great ideas."
- The Mac team included "musicians and poets and artists and zoologists and historians, who also happened to be the best computer scientists in the world." They brought "a very liberal arts attitude" and "I don't think you get that if you are very narrow."
- Asked if he's a hippie or a nerd: "clearly a hippie," and so were the people he worked with. He ties the hippie spark to the sense that life has "something more going on" than a job, a family and two cars in the garage. He says that same spirit, the one that makes people want to be poets instead of bankers, can be put into products, and users can sense it.
- On why Mac users loved the product: the best people he worked with used computers because they were "the medium that is best capable of transmitting some feeling that you have that you want to share with other people."

chunks.heading: NeXT, objects and the web
chunks.text:
- In 1995 Steve ran NeXT, a $50-75M company with about 300 people, the largest supplier of object-oriented technology. He says objects let you build software ten times faster and better.
- His reasoning: innovation was in software, and the Mac made software easier for users but harder to write for developers. Software was a competitive weapon: MCI's Friends & Family was a brilliant idea built on custom billing software, and AT&T took 18 months to respond because it couldn't get its billing software done.
- On the web: it fulfills the dream that the computer would become "a device for communication" rather than computation, and it is exciting "because Microsoft doesn't own it," so there is a lot of innovation.
- He predicted tens of billions of dollars of goods sold on the web. He called it "the ultimate direct to customer distribution channel," where "the smallest company in the world can look as large as the largest company in the world." He expected it to be "the defining social moment for computing."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1990 WGBH interview, Jobs explains why computers are a bicycle of the mind, why the Apple II and Mac won by serving people who wanted to use computers rather than learn them, and why the next revolution is networked interpersonal computing. He argues the best makers are both thinkers and doers, and that market research cannot produce non-incremental leaps.

chunks.heading: The computer as a "bicycle of the mind"
chunks.text:
- Steve recalls a Scientific American article he read at about age twelve that ranked species by the energy (kilocalories) spent to travel from point A to point B. The condor was the most efficient. Humans placed about a third of the way down the list.
- Someone also tested a human on a bicycle, and the human on the bicycle beat the condor, going "all the way off the top of the list."
- His lesson: "we humans are tool builders," and we can build tools that amplify our inherent abilities "to spectacular magnitudes." For him a computer is "a bicycle of the mind," something that "takes us far beyond our inherent abilities."
- He says the computer is still at a very early stage ("we've come only a very short distance") and that what happens in the next hundred years will dwarf what has happened so far.

chunks.heading: What actually drives the industry: three "explosions"
chunks.text:
- Steve says only two things so far have really caused masses of people to buy computers.
  - **Spreadsheets (1977):** Dan Fylstra walked into his office at Apple with a disk from his vest pocket and called it a "visual calculator," which became VisiCalc. He says it propelled the Apple II more than any other single event. Lotus 123 (around 1982) did the same for the IBM PC.
  - **Desktop publishing (1985):** the Macintosh plus the LaserWriter let people do on their desktops what only typesetters and printers could do before.
- The third explosion, which he says is starting in 1990: "let's do for human to human communication what spreadsheets did for financial planning and what desktop publishing did for publishing."
- He calls this **interpersonal computing**. The 1980s were personal computing; networking extends it.
- Multimedia, in his view, is "the means" and not "the end." People will not buy a computer for multimedia. They will buy it for training or interpersonal communication, and voice or video clips will serve that goal. He says computers will stay computers, "just like your toaster isn't your radio," while absorbing the capabilities of other devices.

chunks.heading: Networked organizations and how Steve ran NeXT
chunks.text:
- His argument: business conditions change faster each year, but management hierarchies and geographic organizations cannot. "We can't have somebody working for a new boss every week," or move people around the country every week. An electronic organization can change that fast.
- Networked computers let a cluster of people form around a task with "literally fifteen minutes worth of setup." They can work efficiently regardless of location or reporting line, and the cluster disappears when no longer needed.
- NeXT put a NeXT machine on every employee's desk about 18 months before this interview, linked by high-speed networking. Steve says the revolution he saw there was "larger than the first two."
- His example: for a special project with a company (WGBH), NeXT creates a shared mailbox with about 20 people from marketing, sales, engineering and manufacturing.
  - A message to the mailbox reaches everyone instantly, and replies copy the whole mailbox so everyone reads the "intellectual content going back and forth."
  - Each person gets around 30 messages a day and spends 20 to 30 minutes on them. He says it is "like a beehive."
  - Steve adds his own name to important projects to watch the "disagreements and the arguments and the thoughts and the decisions" fly by. He does background coaching with people he thinks are off track, jumps in on the network if he wants, and takes his name off after a month or so once it is going well.
- Results he claims: at least 50 percent fewer meetings, far more managers and individual contributors involved in decisions, higher-quality decisions, and a "window for management to look into the process of this organism we call our company."
- He wants the computer to work fully standalone too (his example: two weeks in a cabin in Yosemite), then "dock" back into the network and catch up on what happened. He names the seamless transition between standalone and networked use as NeXT's five-year goal.
- He predicts the network will define the home computer market, driving a computer into every house "just like we have a telephone in every house."

chunks.heading: The vision behind NeXT and platform software
chunks.text:
- Steve says everything he has done with computers has been "along pretty much a single vector," and NeXT is another point on it: if computers are the most incredible tools we have built, then "the more powerful tool we can give to people, the more they can do with it."
- He lists three breakthroughs at NeXT:
  - A much more powerful computer for about the same price as a PC.
  - Networking integrated into the computer.
  - A whole new software architecture built from the ground up. He claims it is about ten times as powerful as any PC system and lets applications be built in 25 percent of the time (a quarter of what a PC takes).
- NeXT spent four years with 50 to 100 of the best software people he knew building it.
- On platforms: the industry creates platform software first, then persuades others to write applications on top, and "the height that these new applications can soar is enabled or limited by the platform software." He says only three platforms have ever succeeded in desktop computing (Apple II, IBM PC, Macintosh) and NeXT is attempting the fourth.
- He also frames the personal computer like the automobile versus the passenger train. PCs let millions of people use computers decades earlier and control their own destiny. The cost is that people are "islands," so the challenge is connecting them to get the benefit of both train and car.

chunks.heading: Xerox PARC and the Macintosh: complete the research, then make it affordable
chunks.text:
- Steve first visited Xerox PARC in 1979. He saw larger screens, proportionally spaced text and the mouse (invented by Doug Engelbart at SRI), and it was "instantly obvious to anyone that this was the way things should be." He came back to Apple thinking "our future has just changed."
- The gap: the PARC group had never made a commercial computer and cared more about looking out "fifteen years than ... fifteen months." Menus and other issues were unsolved.
- Apple had to do two things: finish the research ("only about fifty percent complete") and implement it at a cost low enough that people would buy it.
- The Mac was "the computer for the rest of us." The computer is "not an end in itself. It was a means to an end," and most people "didn't want to learn how to use the computer. They just wanted to use it."
- The paradox he describes: to make a computer easier to use you need a more powerful one, because you burn many cycles on ease of use. The easy computer ended up able to do more, and "it took people a few years to figure that out."
- He gives a young-versus-old observation (he mentions Sean Lennon's birthday): older people want to know how it does what it does, while young people just want to know what it can do.
- On the philosophy behind the Mac: it was built by people who felt there was no strict division between science and art, that "mathematics is really a liberal art," and who asked why not bring typography into computers and have computers talk in English. He says the battles to push this out the door "were very large."
- On user interface as a topic: to him it was a natural thing that had to happen, "like automatic transmissions."

chunks.heading: Thinkers and doers, and why people are artists
chunks.text:
- His observation after about 15 years in the industry: "the doers are the major thinkers." The people who change the industry are "both the thinker and doer in one person."
- His example is Leonardo: he did not have someone off to the side thinking about what to paint. Leonardo mixed his own paints, was a good chemist, and knew pigments and human anatomy. Combining art and science, thinking and doing, "was what resulted in the exceptional result."
- He warns it is easy to claim credit for the thinking ("I thought of this three years ago"), but digging deeper usually shows the people who did it also worked through the hard intellectual problems.
- Why the Mac team signed the inside of the case: he considered them artists, "painters and poets" in another era, who now express themselves to their fellow species through the medium of computing.
- The Mac introduction at the shareholders meeting: about 100 to 150 people who made it were in the first rows and cried when the 2,500-person hall gave a standing ovation. He bit his tongue because he had more to present. He says it was emotional because "from that day forward it was no longer ours. We couldn't change it ... It belonged to the world."
- On deadlines: Apple wanted the Mac out a year earlier than it shipped and missed internal deadlines. By the time the Super Bowl spots were bought it was "basically in the bag," but the team worked twenty-four hours a day for the last six months, "on the bomb run."

chunks.heading: Early Apple: shipping assembled, the disk drive, memory, and market research
chunks.text:
- Steve and Woz started Apple because it was the only alternative left: they showed prototypes to Atari (where Steve worked for Nolan Bushnell) and HP (where Woz worked), and both turned them down. "We started the company because it was the only alternative left, not because we wanted to."
- Division of labor: Woz was the brilliant hardware engineer on the core design. Steve worried about which parts to use and how to build and buy them.
- Key decision: sell the main board fully assembled instead of as a kit, which Steve says Apple was first to do. Their reasoning: for every hardware hobbyist there were about a thousand potential software hobbyists, so skipping the soldering opened the product to an order of magnitude more people.
- Three design decisions he credits for the Apple II beating its competition:
  - A reliable, inexpensive floppy disk drive, two to three years ahead of competitors.
  - Up to 48 kilobytes of memory, about three times its competitors, which is why VisiCalc was written for the Apple II. His line: "if Visicalc had been written for some other computer you'd be interviewing somebody else right now."
  - The fully assembled board.
- The moment he knew it would be big: seeing people who could never design a computer, build a kit, assemble a keyboard or write software using them anyway.
- He found Regis McKenna through Intel's advertising ("He told us to go away about four or five times, but eventually he agreed to help us out") and Mike Markkula through a venture capitalist, a month or so before the Apple II was introduced.
- On the 1976 Atlantic City show: a sweltering hotel basement, a hotel table with a tablecloth, a few Apple Is and a homemade poster. The West Coast Computer Faire came about nine months later, with about a hundred companies, and is where the Apple II was introduced.
- **Market research:** In the early days the whole market was in the room at a computer club meeting, and products were simple enough to change in a few months. Later, "market research can tell you what your customers think of something you show them" or want as an incremental improvement, but "very rarely can your customers predict something that they don't even quite know they want yet." No market research could have led to the Macintosh or the personal computer. Once the non-incremental jump has been made, it is a good time to check your instincts with the market.

chunks.heading: Manufacturing, education, and generational change
chunks.text:
- NeXT's automated factory is there mainly to raise quality and shorten time to market, though it also lowers cost. Steve says NeXT was already the lowest-cost producer of its class of product and one of the highest in quality. His view is that to survive in the nineties a company must be world class at both, competing with "Europe Inc. and Japan Inc. and IBM Inc."; he also says the US had forgotten about manufacturing.
- On education: higher education led business by about five years in using networks. ARPANET (funded by DARPA) was handed to universities to "bang on" and improve, and it has tied together the US research community for about a decade. This is why NeXT started out focused exclusively on higher education.
- On K-12: computers there were mostly Apple IIs used for computer literacy, held back by a lack of sophisticated courseware. He wished Macintosh upgrades had come faster.
- On getting from 20 million to 100 million users: "death is the best invention of life" because it brings constant turnover. The best place to make social change is the educational system, so that generations grow up with computers as second nature, just as nearly everyone now drives. In his words: "It's a harsh way of saying it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Onstage with Bill Gates at D5, Jobs explains why Apple stopped treating Microsoft as a zero-sum rival, why it sees itself as a software company, and why it partners instead of doing everything. He closes with advice on passion, scouting talent, and looking forward instead of back.

chunks.heading: Steve and Bill as partners, not rivals
chunks.text:
- Steve credits Bill with building the first software company before most of the industry knew what one was, and with a business model that worked well for the whole industry. He says the biggest thing was that Bill "was really focused on software before almost anybody else had a clue."
- Steve says the two of them stand in for the people behind their companies: "everything that's been done at Microsoft and at Apple has been done by just remarkable people. None of which are sitting up here."
- On the 1997 deal, he says Apple was in serious trouble, and "if the game was a zero sum game, where for Apple to win, Microsoft had to lose, then Apple was going to lose."
- His view was that "Apple wasn't going to beat Microsoft. Apple didn't have to beat Microsoft. Apple had to remember who Apple was, because it'd forgotten who Apple was."
- He argues that too many people at Apple and in its customer base were stuck in that win/lose mindset. He wanted to break it, partly because Microsoft was the biggest outside developer for the Mac.
- He calls the Mac development team at Microsoft one of Apple's best developer relationships.
- On the "I'm a Mac" ads, he says their art "is not to be mean, but it's actually for the guys to like each other." He says "PC guy's great. He's got a big heart."

chunks.heading: Apple as a software company
chunks.text:
- Steve says the iPod exists because the Japanese consumer electronics companies that invented and owned portable music "couldn't conceive of and implement the appropriate software."
- He says "an iPod's really just software." That means software in the device, software on the PC or Mac, and software in the cloud for the store, all "in a beautiful box."
- He applies the same view to the Mac ("it's OS X. It's in a beautiful box") and to the iPhone: "it's software."
- His summary: "Apple views itself as a software company. And there aren't very many software companies left."
- He does not expect the Mac to take 80% of the PC market. Apple is "really happy when our market share goes up a point."
- He quotes Alan Kay: "people that love software want to do their own hardware."
- On hardware and software coupling, he says that in the consumer market, outside of Windows on PCs, it's hard to find examples of decoupled software and hardware working super well. Examples of coupling working well are more common. He admits "nobody knows the answer" yet, and that both approaches may work.

chunks.heading: Rich clients, the cloud and the iPhone Maps example
chunks.text:
- Steve's example is Google Maps on the iPhone. Google provided the back-end data through an API, and Apple wrote the client app.
- The result was "the same set of data coming off the server, but the experience you have using it is unbelievable." He says it blows away any Google Maps client and "you can't do that stuff in a browser."
- His conclusion: "the marriage of some really great client apps with some really great cloud services is incredibly powerful," and right now it can be far more powerful than a browser alone.
- He says the browser is improving at persistent state and offline use, but "it's happening fairly slowly."
- He also notes that hardware is getting good enough to run rich clients on cheaper, lower-power devices.

chunks.heading: Partnering and focus
chunks.text:
- Steve says "we don't think one company can do everything. So you've got to partner with people that are really good at stuff."
- Apple partners on search ("we're not trying to be great at search") and on map back ends, and focuses on being "that consumer's device, and that consumer's experience wrapped around all of this information... in a coherent product."
- He builds a service itself only when nothing good exists. For iTunes, "there wasn't a music delivery service that was any good. And we had to do one, so we'll do one."
- He says "life's complex," and that it's "really hard for one company to do everything."
- He concedes that Apple was not good at partnering early on because Woz and he "started the company based on doing the whole banana."
- By contrast, he says Bill and Microsoft "learned how to partner with people really well." Steve says Apple would have been well served by more of that, and didn't learn it until a few decades later.

chunks.heading: Where PCs and post-PC devices are heading
chunks.text:
- Steve describes the PC as resilient and as having been reborn several times: first as the productivity machine, then as the internet machine, then as the "digital hub" for cameras, camcorders and sharing.
- He expects the PC, as a general-purpose device, to keep morphing (tablet, notebook, desktop) and to be tied more tightly to back-end internet services.
