- Macintosh is "the first 'telephone' of our industry."
- Principle: a tool that demands specialized training before it is useful will not reach most people. Ease of use is the precondition for mass adoption.

chunks.heading: Letting people "sing": expressiveness as the point of the Mac
chunks.text:
- Steve's favorite thing about the telephone over the telegraph is that it let you sing and "intone your words with meaning beyond the simple linguistics."
- Macintosh does the same: "Macintosh lets you sing."
- Concrete examples he gives:
  - Memos in Times Roman or Helvetica, a serious font for something serious, or an Old English font for fun (a volleyball announcement).
  - Drawings and pictures, including other people's, incorporated into documents.
- "And you can express yourself."
- He sees the computer as a medium of expression, not only a productivity tool.

chunks.heading: Better communication and more fun at work
chunks.text:
- In business, five-page memos are compressed into one-page memos because a picture expresses the key concept.
- Result: "less paper flying around and more quality of communication."
- He calls Macintosh "more fun" and rejects the myth that fun people at home become "dull and boring and serious" at work: "it's simply not true."
- His goal: inject "that liberal-arts spirit into this very serious realm of business," which he thinks "would be a worthwhile contribution."
- Principle: technology joined with the liberal arts, aimed at ordinary people rather than specialists.

chunks.heading: The IBM story: how Steve framed the competitive landscape (Oct 1983 sales meeting)
chunks.text:
Steve told Apple's sales force a short history of IBM repeatedly dismissing new categories:
- 1958: IBM passed up the chance to buy a young company that had invented xerography. Two years later, Xerox was born. "IBM has been kicking themselves ever since."
- Late 1960s: DEC and others invented the minicomputer. IBM dismissed it as too small for serious computing. DEC grew into a multi-hundred-million-dollar corporation before IBM entered.
- Late 1970s: Apple, a young company, invented the Apple II in 1977, "the first personal computer as we know it today." IBM again dismissed it as too small and unimportant.
- 1981: Apple II became the world's most popular computer. Apple had grown to a $300 million company, the fastest-growing corporation in American business history, with over fifty competitors. IBM entered in November 1981 with the IBM PC.

chunks.heading: The 1983 market numbers and the stakes
chunks.text:
- In 1983, Apple and IBM each sold roughly one billion dollars' worth of personal computers.
- In 1984, each would invest more than $50 million in R&D and another $50 million in TV advertising, almost a quarter of a billion dollars combined.
- The industry shakeout was in full swing: the first major firm went bankrupt, others teetered, and total industry losses for 1983 outweighed even the combined PC profits of Apple and IBM.
- His framing of 1984: IBM "wants it all" and is aiming at its last obstacle, Apple. Dealers who welcomed IBM now fear an IBM-dominated future and are "desperately turning back to Apple" as the force that can ensure their freedom.
- He rallies the room with questions: will Big Blue dominate the entire computer industry, the entire information age? "Was George Orwell right about 1984?"

chunks.heading: The "1984" commercial and its rollout
chunks.text:
- Steve introduced the ad at an Apple sales meeting in October 1983, before showing it to the room.
- Directed by Ridley Scott: gray, shaven-headed people watch a dictator on a giant screen; a woman in bright red shorts and a Macintosh shirt hurls a hammer through it.
- The closing line: "On January 24th, Apple Computer will introduce Macintosh. And you'll see why 1984 won't be like '1984.'"
- It was set to run one week before the Macintosh introduction (it ran during the 1984 Super Bowl).
- The audience responded with tumultuous applause and shouting.
- Steve credited the ad agency Chiat/Day, who were in the room: Jay Chiat (principal), and Lee Clow and Steve Hayden, who wrote the copy and did the creative.
- Takeaway: he cast Apple's launch as a cause (freedom from a dominant incumbent) rather than a feature list, and he gave public credit to the creative team.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a May 1984 interview, Jobs says his taste is ordinary but his stubbornness isn't: making something great costs little extra beyond time and perseverance. He describes aesthetics as a trained eye refined by mistakes, and pushes for smaller, simpler, more precise products.

chunks.heading: How Steve's taste in design develops
chunks.text:
- Steve says his aesthetic taste is not unusual: "I don't think my taste in aesthetics is that much different than a lot of other people's."
- His influences were many small things, not any one profound source: wine labels, paintings in galleries, Volkswagen Beetles and vans. While designing the Mac he went around looking at Cuisinarts ("my Cuisinart week").
- The difference is that he is stubborn about making things as good as everyone knows they can be.
- Taste improves through mistakes: "Things get more refined as you make mistakes... Your aesthetics get better as you make mistakes."
- He compares aesthetics to singing. Joan Baez's voice is beautiful because of her superb ear (she can imitate a voice after thirty seconds of listening). In the same way, good aesthetics come from the eye, from an instinct for what you see, not so much from what you do.

chunks.heading: Making things great costs time, not money
chunks.text:
- "If you're going to make something, it doesn't take any more energy—and rarely does it take more money—to make it really great."
- All it takes is a little more time, not much more, and a willingness to persevere until it is really great.
- He sees this willingness to persevere as the real difference between good and great products.

chunks.heading: Smaller products allow more precision
chunks.text:
- Steve wants to build products inherently smaller than anything on the market.
- Smaller things can be made more precisely. His example is a watch: it is beautiful because its precision matches the scale of the object.
- As Apple's products shrink, the company gets the chance to express their form more precisely.
- He wants everything to be smaller.

chunks.heading: Products you can pick up and carry
chunks.text:
- Even products that are not truly portable should have a handle that says "Pick me up and move me when you want to change where I am."
- Users should be able to carry them from room to room, office to office, or home for the weekend.
- Lisa was too heavy for this. The question for the future is how to package the same functionality into something smaller that people can carry, with the form expressed more precisely.

chunks.heading: Ugly everyday products and the push for simplicity
chunks.text:
- Steve says most designed things around us are ugly: most cars (any car before three years ago), tables, chairs, and nearly everything in the room.
- Telephones are his example: only the original phone and the Trimline were any good. The Trimline is "the only decent one." What was done to newer phones is "just garbage."
- His direction for Apple: "we're just getting simpler and simpler and simpler. Very, very simple."

chunks.heading: Natural light in the workplace
chunks.text:
- He admires HP's original buildings on Page Mill Road. They have scalloped roofs with glass facing north, which gives a whole glass wall, tons of natural light for the people working inside, and could even take solar collectors.
- He criticizes Apple's own buildings as dark: after five minutes outside, you walk in and can't see anything, "living in these little tiny caverns."
- He wants "a ton of natural light."

chunks.heading: What the "1984" commercial was saying
chunks.text:
- Steve endorses Fortune's response about the Big Brother and IBM reading: "If seeing Big Brother in 1984 connotes IBM to a large number of people, that says more about IBM's image problem than our intentions."
- He admits Apple saw the analogy, and that "you'd have to be an idiot not to see the parallels to IBM."
- The first message was a comment on the cultural fear of computers as powerful machines controlled by a centralized group of people to keep track of us.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Weeks after leaving Apple, Jobs explains why he wants to keep making things rather than become a pundit or professor, how he measures success by raising the bar for computers, and how he coped with the humiliation. He says Apple lives in its people's spirit and that he is not bitter.

chunks.heading: Losing Apple and the drive to keep building
chunks.text:
- Steve had hoped his life with Apple would be "an interesting tapestry" in which he weaved in and out. He would be there for a period, go off and contribute elsewhere while staying connected, then perhaps return for a lengthy stretch.
- He says it did not work out that way, but still calls it "ten of the best years of my life" and says he doesn't "regret much of anything."
- He could not have imagined the ending "in my wildest imagination."

chunks.heading: Why he wants to build, not teach or comment
chunks.text:
- At thirty, Steve says "I want to build things" and is "not ready to be an industry pundit."
- He turned down three offers to be a professor that summer, telling the universities he "would be an awful professor."
- His self-assessment: "What I'm best at doing is finding a group of talented people and making things with them."
- He respects the direction Apple is going, but he wants to make things himself.
- If there is no place for him to make things at Apple, he will do what he did twice before: "I'll make my own place." He built in the garage when Apple started, and in the "metaphorical garage" when the Mac started.

chunks.heading: His yardstick for success
chunks.text:
- Steve says the outside world measures success numerically, but his yardstick is different.
- His measure is that every computer designed from here on out will have to be at least as good as a Macintosh.
- Success for him is raising the standard for the whole industry, not revenue or market share.

chunks.heading: What Apple is, and what losing it would mean
chunks.text:
- Steve says Apple "exists in the spirit of the people that work there" and in the philosophies and purpose by which they go about their business.
- He would feel he had lost Apple only if it became a place where computers are a commodity item, where "the romance is gone," and where people forget that computers are "the most incredible invention that man has ever invented."
- If he were "a million miles away" and those people still felt that way and were working on the next great personal computer, he would feel "my genes are still in there."

chunks.heading: Being sidelined, and how he coped
chunks.text:
- In June and July he went to work with only a call or two and a little mail. Most corporate management reports stopped crossing his desk.
- He would get "really depressed," go home after three or four hours, and eventually judged that routine "mentally unhealthy," so he stopped going in. "There was nobody really there to miss me."
- One of his five most difficult days was when John Sculley told analysts there was no future role for him, and repeated it at another analyst meeting a week later. Sculley said it to the press, not to Steve directly.
- Steve compares it to being punched in the stomach: you can't breathe until you relax. That was how he felt all summer, and the task was to try to relax.
- His response was long walks in the woods and not talking to many people.

chunks.heading: Owning his rough edges without apologizing for who he is
chunks.text:
- Asked whether he contributed to his own downfall, Steve says he is not "a sixty-two-year-old statesman that's traveled around the world all his life."
- He is sure there were situations at twenty-five he could have handled much better knowing what he knows now. He expects to say the same at thirty-five about 1985.
- "I can be very intense in my convictions." He adds: "all in all, I kind of like myself, and I'm not that anxious to change."
- He says the experience is changing him: "I think I am growing from this, and I think I'm learning a lot from it," though he isn't sure yet how or what.
- He repeats, "I'm not bitter."

chunks.heading: Buddhism, monasteries, and staying in America
chunks.text:
- On press interest in his Buddhism and vegetarianism, he jokes about descending "into the isms." He says he doesn't eat meat and doesn't go to church every Sunday.
- He had considered going to Japan to sit in a monastery and says he is glad he didn't.
- He admits it will sound "really, really corny," but he feels American and was born here.
- He believes "the fate of the world is in America's hands right now," and says he will live his life here and "do what I can to help."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Short writings by Steve on the origin of NeXT (a lunch with biochemist Paul Berg), why Pixar's graphics work drew him in, and Pixar's early strategy. He reflects that trying to pay the bills with side products was the wrong approach, and that the goal was technology so good nobody needs to understand it to love the result.

chunks.heading: NeXT's origin came from a conversation with a biochemist
chunks.text:
- Weeks after founding NeXT, Steve told Newsweek the original insight came from reading biochemistry and recombinant DNA literature.
- He called Paul Berg, a pioneer of recombinant DNA techniques, said "I'm ignorant about this stuff, but I've got a bunch of questions about how it works," and asked him to lunch at Stanford.
- Berg showed him how gene repair experiments ran in a wet laboratory, taking a week or two or three each.
- Steve noticed the work "smells a lot like some of the concepts you find in computer science."
- He asked, "Why don't you simulate these on a computer?" His reasoning: experiments would run faster, and "someday every freshman microbiology student in the country can play with the Paul Berg recombinant software."
- He called it "a landmark lunch" because it got his "wheels turning again."
- The pattern: he cold-called an expert in a field he was ignorant of, asked naive questions, and found where computing could transform their workflow.

chunks.heading: What drew Steve to Pixar: graphics well beyond anything he had seen
chunks.text:
- Steve met Ed Catmull, who ran the computer division of Lucasfilm, in 1985.
- He had been involved in graphics most of his life:
  - The Apple II was "the first real color computer that you could get your hands on."
  - The Macintosh was graphics.
  - The LaserWriter was graphics.
- All of that was 2-D. Apple had done some 3-D work and he knew the field.
- Even so, what Catmull's team was doing was "way ahead of anything I'd ever seen anyone do."
- He was drawn by a team clearly ahead of the state of the art in a field he already knew well.

chunks.heading: Pixar's early strategy failed: pay the bills with products
chunks.text:
- In 2003 Steve told filmmaker Leslie Iwerks the early strategy was "find a way to pay the bills."
- In the background, Pixar developed animation software, and John Lasseter made a succession of short films on the way to Toy Story.
- The company tried to fund itself with other products, such as the Pixar Image Computer and software, to "just buy time."
- Steve's verdict: "That strategy really turned out not to work."
- In hindsight: "we would have been better off just funding the animation efforts and not trying to pay the bills through these other products."
- In the end, "I just ended up writing checks to keep the company going," which went on for ten years.
- The lesson: funding the core creative work directly beats distracting the company with side products to cover costs.

chunks.heading: Technology should disappear into the experience
chunks.text:
- Steve saw "magic" in Pixar's short films from the beginning.
- Most Pixar technology required expertise to appreciate, but "you didn't have to know anything about the technology to enjoy the film."
- He called this "incredibly refreshing" and said it "pointed the way to where we wanted to go."
- The principle: "We didn't want to have to convince people that our technology was great — we knew it was great."
- The goal was "to use our technology to make something where nobody needed to know anything about the technology to love it."
- That is what Pixar ended up doing.

chunks.heading: Celebrating Tin Toy: team credit and an industry milestone (1989)
chunks.text:
- On March 30, 1989, Steve emailed all NeXT employees after the Academy Awards under the subject "A great day and a half."
- He congratulated everyone "for a real TEAM effort" at NeXT, and noted Pixar had won too.
- Pixar won the short animated film Oscar for Tin Toy, the first computer-generated film ever to win an Academy Award.
- It beat several very good traditionally animated films.
- His framing: "The computer graphics industry just achieved a major milestone, and Pixar led the way!"
- He shared a win from a sister company with his whole NeXT team, treating it as a shared achievement and a proof point for his belief in computer graphics.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Speaking to incoming Reed freshmen while NeXT struggled and Pixar had layoffs, Jobs recounts dropping in on classes, living hungry, and the generosity of dean Jack Dudman. He credits humanities study and adversity for shaping his character and for everything he later built.

chunks.heading: Hunger as a school for character
chunks.text:
- Steve ties character to adversity: "Character is built not in good times, but in bad times; not in a time of plenty, but in a time of adversity."
- He credits Reed with nurturing that spirit of adversity and says it "does build some character."
- He closes by thanking the school "for teaching me how to be hungry and how to keep that with me my whole life."
- He gave the speech on August 27, 1991, when NeXT computers were not selling well and Pixar had just had a round of layoffs. He was speaking from a hard stretch himself.

chunks.heading: Why the humanities mattered in hindsight
chunks.text:
- Steve was forced to attend humanities lectures "it seemed like every day" and studied Shakespeare with Professor Svitavsky.
- At the time he thought they were "meaningless and even somewhat cruel endeavors to be put through."
- With time he came to thank God for them: "It has helped me in everything I've ever done, although I wouldn't have ever guessed it at the time."
- He argues that the value of such study shows up only years later, once "the patina of time takes its toll," and that it can't be judged in the moment.

chunks.heading: Dropping out and dropping in
chunks.text:
- He ran out of money after one semester at Reed and dropped out.
- He then dropped in for another year and a half, so he stayed "by choice."
- He never graduated, and says that makes him an unusual but not unique alumnus.
- During that time he stayed on campus without paying and took classes without being a formal student or paying tuition.
- Experiences from Reed "have stayed with me my whole life."

chunks.heading: Living on almost nothing
chunks.text:
- He was hungry "all the time." The cafeteria taught him quickly to be a vegetarian.
- He gathered Coke bottles and returned them to the store for money to eat.
- The cheapest food he found was Roman Meal, a cereal. He lived on it for many months.
- Several friends hitchhiked across town on Sundays to the Hare Krishna temple, which fed all comers. After days without eating, they timed their arrival for after the religious practices and just before the food.
- Steve treats this scarcity as formative rather than something to regret.

chunks.heading: Situational ethics from the Hare Krishnas
chunks.text:
- After meals he and friends sometimes stayed over, too full to move. The temple woke them at 4 a.m. to gather flowers to honor Krishna.
- The group stole flowers from neighbors' gardens. Neighbors learned to guard their beds, so the group had to range in a wider circle around the temple.
- They also sold incense to local department stores and stole it back, so the stores would buy more.
- Their ethics held that "anything in the service of Krishna was fine."
- Steve says that in interacting with them, "I think I learned more about situational ethics than I ever did on campus."

chunks.heading: Generosity from Jack Dudman
chunks.text:
- Jack Dudman, then dean of Reed, was "one of the heroes of my life" while Steve was there.
- Dudman looked the other way while Steve stayed on campus without paying and took classes without paying tuition.
- When Steve was "at the end of my rope," Dudman would walk with him, and Steve would later find a twenty-dollar bill in his tattered coat pocket, with no mention from Jack before, during, or after.
- Steve says: "I learned more about generosity from Jack Dudman and the people here at this school than I learned anywhere else in my life."

chunks.heading: A perspective on age and return
chunks.text:
- Steve says people's "spark of self-consciousness" turns on at about fifteen or sixteen.
- Normalizing age to that point, he says the freshmen are two to four years old and he is about twenty.
- He frames his return to Reed as a look back on formative experiences, offered as things that "maybe could be of some value."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1995 email thread, Steve Jobs first demands compensation from Intel for Pixar's hard-won graphics knowledge, then reverses 180 degrees after Andy Grove explains that friends help each other without keeping score. It shows Jobs valuing expertise, defending the worth of ten years of invested work, and admitting he was wrong.

chunks.heading: Reciprocity over transactional pricing: Steve's 180-degree reversal with Andy Grove (1995)
chunks.text:
- Pixar built its 3D graphics "secrets" through "significant investment over ten years or more." Steve believed they could let Intel's general-purpose processors render 3D graphics well enough to beat dedicated gaming machines (Sega, Nintendo, Playstation) and dramatically enlarge the PC's consumer market share.
- His initial position was commercial: disclosing the "correct" way to do high-quality, high-performance graphics would cost Pixar its competitive advantage, "with no work on their part" from competitors, "hence, the need for compensation." He asked Intel: "What does Intel propose to give Pixar for disclosing and licensing its secrets to Intel?"
- He argued that anyone about to "make hundreds of millions of something" should be willing to pay "for the best advice money could buy."
- After an Intel engineer replied that Intel had never paid for ideas, Steve fired back that this approach "has not served you well in the past, as evidenced by your poor graphics architectures and performance." He privately called the engineer's approach "extremely arrogant."

chunks.heading: How Andy Grove changed his mind
chunks.text:
- Grove sided firmly with his engineer. The engineer had taken Steve's offer to help seriously and "rounded up the best technical people" before Steve "introduced a brand new element into the discussion: money."
- Grove's argument was from precedent and friendship: he had offered Steve free advice, from porting NextStep to the 486 to presenting on repositioning NextStep to Steve's staff, and "it never entered my mind to charge for it."
- His principle: "that's what friendly companies (and friends) do for each other. In the long run, these things balance out."
- He warned that refusing would leave Intel "worse off... and so will the industry."

chunks.heading: Steve's reversal
chunks.text:
- Steve answered within days: "I have many faults, but one of them is not ingratitude. And, I do agree with you that 'In the long run, these things balance out.'"
- He declared "I have changed my position 180 degrees" and committed to freely help the engineer make Intel's processors "much better for 3D graphics."
- He arranged for the Pixar technical team to meet as soon as they could be "freed up from the film," so the film still came first.
- He thanked Grove for "the clearer perspective."

chunks.heading: Takeaways on leadership and mindset
chunks.text:
- Steve could hold a hard, even combative line on the value of Pixar's work, then reverse completely when a mentor reframed the relationship.
- He weighed gratitude and past help (Grove had helped NeXT) against short-term deal logic, and the mentor's reminder was enough to change course.
- He accepted correction from someone he respected, quickly and without face-saving, and acknowledged the new perspective in writing.
- Context: Steve and Grove were close enough that Steve could write candidly ("this isn't a sales pitch; I just wanted you to know what I thought, as always") and Grove could answer bluntly in return.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In 1996, after Pixar's Toy Story success, Jobs reflects on being ousted from Apple and not fearing failure, why Apple lost its ten-year lead by ceasing to innovate, and how Apple's real contribution was a liberal arts view of computing. He also describes a bottoms-up culture where great hires tell you what to do, and says work and life are the same thing.

chunks.heading: Why Steve bets on Toy Story: the milestone email to Pixar (January 1996)
chunks.text:
- On Jan 2, 1996, Steve emailed Pixar that Toy Story had crossed $150M domestic box office, "only 13 days after crossing $100M".
- He called it "the undisputed blockbuster of the holiday season," topping Jumanji, Father of the Bride II, Waiting to Exhale and Balto.
- He flagged it could become the top film of 1995, passing Batman Forever ($184M) and Apollo 13 ($172M).
- It was already the third most successful animated feature ever, behind only Aladdin ($217M) and The Lion King ($312M).
- He closed with a rallying call to the team: "To $175M and beyond!" and "Congratulations team."

chunks.heading: The web as a leveling, direct-to-customer channel
chunks.text:
- Steve sees the web as "the ultimate direct-to-customer distribution chain, bypassing all middlemen," going straight from supplier to consumer.
- A small company that invests heavily in its website "can look just as formidable and just as solid on the web as a very large company." Some small companies were hipper to the web sooner and looked better than large ones.
- He calls it "a very leveling phenomenon": goods, services and demand creation would increasingly happen over the web.
- It is also shopping for information. He checks local movie listings on a web page rather than the newspaper or calling theaters.
- Example: he bought a Sony camcorder by researching Sony's web page first. "The demand to get me to buy that thing was created from Sony's web page."
- He expects people to make more life and purchase decisions from the web.
- Special-interest groups can form around information that never existed before, such as web pages for stroke victims covering the latest treatments and avoidance advice.

chunks.heading: Software distribution and post-PC devices
chunks.text:
- Steve says there is "no question" software will be downloaded from the web, and he expected it within twenty-four months.
- The bottleneck is the last mile: corporate on-ramps are fast, but off-ramps to consumers' homes are slow. Large CD-ROM games would stay on physical media for a while, until faster links such as cable modems arrive.
- PCs will be around for quite some time, but he asks whether the first successful post-PC devices are near. PDAs tried and failed.
- His next candidate is a low-cost consumer internet appliance: a three-hundred-dollar box that connects to the TV on one side and ISDN or a cable modem on the other, giving a web browser in the living room.
- He wants innovative marketing and distribution around such devices so many people suddenly have a browser at home, and calls it "the beginning of the first real post-PC market."

chunks.heading: Not being afraid to fail
chunks.text:
- Being forced out of Apple, the company he created, was "a very painful time," but "you just march forward, and you try to learn from it."
- His self-coaching: "not being afraid to fail."
- After a failure, people get protective and never want to fall on their face again. He calls that "a big mistake, because you never achieve what you want without falling on your face a few times in the process of getting there."
- He says he has "failed quite a bit since leaving Apple."

chunks.heading: Why Apple lost its lead: the failure to keep innovating
chunks.text:
- When he left Apple, it had a ten-year lead over Microsoft, which he says comes along maybe once every few decades (Xerox, IBM with mainframes). Apple's was the graphical user interface.
- "The problem at Apple was that they stopped innovating." The Mac shipping in 1996 was "25 percent different than the day I left," not enough for ten years and billions in R&D.
- Microsoft wasn't brilliant in copying; "the Mac was a sitting duck for ten years." Apple's differentiation evaporated.
- Compaq and other Intel-Microsoft makers need only be 5 percent better to win. Apple, being outside the mainstream, must be 50 or 100 percent better, because buyers take a risk and want a much bigger reward.
- Cost-cutting is not the cure. "The cure for Apple is to innovate its way out," and good people remain who can do it "with the proper leadership, which is what's been missing."
- He tries not to talk about Apple much. He is happy every time a Mac ships and compares it to a first love: you can't always stay in love with your first girlfriend.

chunks.heading: The liberal arts point of view in computing
chunks.text:
- Steve says he expects another group would have achieved similar things eventually, but Apple was in the right place, at the right time, with the right team.
- Apple's major contribution: "bringing a liberal arts point of view to the use of computers."
- The Mac's driving motivation was ease of use for many more people on nontraditional tasks, beautiful fonts and typography, and graphics for seeing photographs and artwork, "not for plotting laminar flow calculations."
- The goal was "a liberal arts perspective and a liberal arts audience" for what had been a "very geeky technology and a very geeky audience."
- Based on how he was raised, he believes "science and computer science is a liberal art": something everyone should know how to use, "not something that should be relegated to 5 percent of the population over in the corner."
- "That's the seed of Apple: computers for the rest of us." He thinks the liberal arts view still lives at Apple but not many other places, and says Microsoft took ten years to copy the Mac because "they didn't really get it at its core."

chunks.heading: Company culture: great ideas from anywhere, hire people to tell you what to do
chunks.text:
- Apple was a corporation, driven to make money "so that we could continue to invest in the things we loved."
- Its big difference: "a real belief that there wasn't a hierarchy of ideas that mapped onto the hierarchy of the organization." Great ideas could come from anywhere, and people were treated in an egalitarian way regarding where ideas came from.
- Apple was "a very bottoms-up company" for many great ideas.
- "We hired truly great people and gave them the room to do great work." Many companies "hire people to tell them what to do. We hired people to tell us what to do."
- The result was a culture "much more collegial than hierarchical."

chunks.heading: Work and life
chunks.text:
- Early Apple was young and mostly unmarried, so people worked fifteen-hour days. "Your work was your life, in many cases."
- Steve says work is still his life but not all of it. "I've never been able to think of my work and my life as different things. They're the same thing."
- Work was 99 percent of his life then and is maybe 50 percent now.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1996 graduation speech, Jobs urges students to trust their intuitions, gather diverse experiences so they can connect dots others miss, and refuse the "career" in favor of making what they love their work. He frames life as a rainbow where the journey is the reward, and mortality as the reason to blaze.

chunks.heading: Follow your intuitions, not a "career"
chunks.text:
Steve told the graduating class that the most important things in life are not the goal-oriented, materialistic things everyone urges you to chase. He asks students to stay alert to life's "magical, mystical, and artistic sides."

- He says people rarely learn to listen to their intuitions, and that you can "make them come true" if you pay attention.
- A way to hear them: walk alone near sunset and spend time looking at the sky.
- The images he lists (sculpting in Paris, running a hospital for poor children in India, recording an album, working out a law of physics alone at 4:30 a.m.) are the kind of feelings he says are "very real" and can "blossom into something wonderful and magical."
- If you have no such dreams, he says you are "in trouble" and should recapture them before spending four or more years on a direction your heart may not want.

chunks.heading: Ignore the people who say your dream is impractical
chunks.text:
He expects people to argue against following those feelings, and answers with examples:

- "You can't make a living writing songs." (Bob Dylan)
- "Helping children in India is nice, but you need to prepare for real life." (Mother Teresa)
- "You could be doing so much more with your life." He cites Einstein, working a low-level job in the Swiss patent office rather than teaching at a university, so he could stay up late working through his new ideas.

chunks.heading: Creativity is connecting unrelated experiences
chunks.text:
- Definition: "Creativity equals connecting previously unrelated experiences and insights that others don't see."
- "You have to have them to connect them." Creative people often feel guilty that they are simply relaying what they "see."
- You get a more diverse set of experiences by not "traveling the same path as everyone else."
- He advises you to "feed" or "invest" in yourself by exploring uncharted paths outside your past experience, especially "those that carry a romantic scent."
- No one can know in advance which paths lead anywhere. The only thing to do is believe that "some of what you follow with your heart will indeed come back to make your life much richer." Doing so builds "an ever firmer trust in your instincts and intuition."

chunks.heading: The calligraphy class that shaped the Macintosh
chunks.text:
Steve's example of connecting dots:

- At Reed College, a small liberal arts college in Portland, Oregon, then the center of a US calligraphy revival, he took a calligraphy course before leaving. At eighteen he was exposed to typography, graphic layout and font design.
- There was no hope of income from it, and some friends derided him for wasting his time on "fancy letters."
- Years later, designing the Macintosh, that experience drove him to insist on proportionally spaced type and a range of fonts, bringing a much richer typography to computers than had existed.
- It also led to the LaserWriter printer, so the letterforms could be printed at the quality they deserved, which "set the stage for 'desktop publishing.'"
- His claim: none of this would have happened at Apple if he had skipped that class for a more "substantive" one in economics or engineering.

chunks.heading: Don't be a career: make your avocation your vocation
chunks.text:
- He calls the "Career" one of "the most dangerous and stifling concepts ever invented by humans," and the enemy of most dreams and intuitions. It is a concept of progressing through stages while training for and practicing your working life.
- The first problem is the notion that work is separate from the rest of life. If you are passionate about both, "they will become more or less one," which he calls a much better way to live.
- The perceived risk goes down as you meet the real world. Many people pick what they think are safe harbors (he names lawyers and accountants) and wake up ten or fifteen years later to discover the price they paid.
- His instruction: "Make your avocation your vocation. Make what you love your work."

chunks.heading: The journey is the reward
chunks.text:
- People think you've made it at the end of the rainbow with the pot of gold. He says the reward is in crossing the rainbow.
- He notes he got the pot of gold "(literally)", and that anyone who reaches it knows it isn't the reward, so they go looking for another rainbow to cross.
- He asks students to think of life as a rainbow arcing across the horizon: you appear, get a chance to blaze in the sky, then disappear.
- The endpoints are birth and death, both experienced completely alone. He thinks young people are sheltered from both, out of fear that mortality will wound them.
- For him it is the opposite: "to know my arc will fall makes me want to blaze while I am in the sky. Not for others, but for myself, for the trail I know I am leaving."

chunks.heading: Regrets versus mistakes
chunks.text:
- Mistakes are things you did and wish you could do over. Sometimes you were a fool, scared, or hurt someone. Some are deep, others not, but "if your intent was pure, they are almost always enriching in some way."
- Regrets are "most often things you didn't do, and wish you did." The goal is to live your arc with as few regrets as possible.
- His example: he still regrets not kissing Nancy Kinniman in high school.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1996 interview Jobs explains his role at Pixar as creating the environment where top creative and technical talent can do their best work, why Pixar avoids contracts, and why storytelling, not technology, makes films last. Two short emails show him persuading a team to join the holiday waltz and announcing Apple's acquisition of NeXT.

chunks.heading: Building a studio around talent, not contracts
chunks.text:
- Steve says he is "not a filmmaker" and doesn't direct Pixar's films. His job is to help "create the environment where all these incredible people can make films."
- Pixar's edge: the very best creative people will only work at a few places (Disney, Pixar, possibly DreamWorks), and the very best computer graphics scientists likewise. He argues Pixar is "the only place in the world that can hire the best from both of these areas."
- It took ten years to get both groups working together, because Hollywood culture and Silicon Valley culture are really different. Pixar tried to pick "the best from both."
- His role, as he describes it: understand the pieces needed to build a pure-play feature animation studio, attract and retain the people, get a clear strategy in place, and help with the relationship with Disney.
- He says his greatest joy is working with people much better than him at something, so he can stop worrying about it and move on to where he can help.
- He says Pixar is small and "we don't want to let any of this go to our heads."

chunks.heading: No contracts: retention through stock and daily effort
chunks.text:
- Steve contrasts two retention models. Hollywood uses the stick, the contract. Silicon Valley uses the carrot, the stock option. Pixar examined both economically, psychologically and culturally, and chose the Silicon Valley model.
- Stock aligns everyone on one goal: creating shareholder value.
- Lack of contracts forces constant effort: "Every single day we worry about how we can make Pixar a better company so that nobody will ever want to leave, and so we don't take anybody for granted."
- He criticizes the contract mindset: a sophisticated manager sets a database reminder six months before a contract ends, treats the person as "the most important person in the world for six months," and after they re-sign, "you put them in a drawer."
- His view: if someone doesn't want to be at Pixar, they should probably leave anyway, contract or not.

chunks.heading: Inverted hierarchy: management serves the talent
chunks.text:
- In technology and in Pixar's creative side, talented people are rare and in demand, and "if you don't treat them right, they can go get another job in ten minutes."
- As a result, "the hierarchy of power sort of inverts, and the CEO is actually at the bottom." He says he feels he works for most of these people because they do the brilliant work.
- Same in software: the best people are very hard to come by, so it's management's job to support them on the front lines.

chunks.heading: Editing the film before you make it
chunks.text:
- In live action, a director typically shoots ten to twenty-five times as much footage as ends up on screen, and edits afterward.
- Animation is too expensive for that. Disney realized decades ago that you can't afford to animate ten times what you need, "you don't want to animate even 10 percent more than what you need." The conclusion: "you have to edit your film before you make it."
- Disney pioneered and refined techniques for this over sixty years. Working with Disney gave Pixar access to "wisdom that you can't buy for love or money," from having made tens of feature animated films.

chunks.heading: Technology grows ambition, but story is the art
chunks.text:
- Render times: on the short film Luxo Jr. ten years earlier, each frame took about three hours on average. Computers are now a hundred times faster, yet Toy Story still took about three hours per frame, because frames were up to a hundred times more complex.
- For the second feature, code name Bugs, Pixar is throwing five to ten times more computer power than Toy Story at it, and it will still take about three hours per frame. "Our ambitions visually are growing as fast as the technology can feed them."
- On the creative side: "no amount of technology can turn a bad story into a good story." Storytelling is a very old art, he doesn't think it has changed in a long time, and it has nothing to do with the technology. Pixar will keep working on it "very, very hard."

chunks.heading: Why stories outlast technology
chunks.text:
- Technology products have short lives: an Apple II is hard to find outside schools, and it's unclear a Macintosh could be booted five years later. A year or two is typical, five is extraordinary, ten to fifteen is rare. They become "sedimentary layer" for new innovation.
- By contrast, Disney released Snow White in 1937. A few years before this interview, a video rerelease sold 28 million copies, probably around a quarter billion dollars of profit, sixty years after release.
- Watching his young son watch Snow White thirty or forty times, he saw that these stories "renew themselves with each generation of young children." He cites Joseph Campbell: these are our myths.
- His prediction: people will watch Toy Story in sixty years, "not because of the computer graphics, but because of the story about friendship."
- He calls the chance to "put these stories into the culture" a rare opportunity, and says everyone at Pixar feels privileged.

chunks.heading: Internal emails: culture and the NeXT deal (December 1996)
chunks.text:
- **Holiday Waltz (Dec 12, 1996):** About 40 people felt uncomfortable attending because they lacked a guest or thought it too formal. Steve's pitch: that's exactly why it will be fun, a chance to see colleagues "in a strange costume (tuxedo) doing a totally foreign activity (waltzing)." He notes his own last waltz was ten years earlier, says cutting in during a waltz is "proper and flattering" for singles, and closes with "We will miss you if you don't come. What do you have to lose?"
- **Apple acquires NeXT (Dec 20, 1996):** He tells Pixar staff the deal is good for Apple (a very advanced object-oriented OS, OpenStep, that can "leapfrog Microsoft Windows"), for NeXT (OpenStep going mainstream, a ten-year dream), for Pixar (it frees him from running two companies so he can devote more energy to Pixar, with possible future Apple-Pixar collaboration "if creatively driven"), and for himself. He will advise Apple on product strategy and spend even more time at Pixar.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1990s interview for a Stanford-student book, Jobs explains why great people come first, why he spends a fifth of his time recruiting, and how he spots A players by their results and how they hold up under pressure. He also reflects on his liberal arts strength, his idealism, and why the work itself motivates teams.

chunks.heading: Hiring is the highest-leverage work, and quality starts with people
chunks.text:
- Steve says "You'd better have great people, or you won't get your product to market as fast as possible." Weak teams either ship late or ship fast but "really clunky" products nobody buys.
- "There are no shortcuts around quality, and quality starts with people." He adds that maybe shortcuts exist, but he is "not smart enough to have ever found any."
- He spends 20 percent of his time recruiting, even at the time of this interview (1997). He also spends a day a week helping other people recruit.
- He calls recruiting "one of the most important things you can do."

chunks.heading: How to identify A players: results first, potential second
chunks.text:
- He admits it is "a very hard question" and describes two paths.
- **Experienced candidates:** judge by results. Some people "look so good on paper and talk such a good story but have no results behind them." They cannot point to breakthroughs or shipped products where they played an integral part.
- **Reverse search:** he finds great people by looking at great results, then finding out who was responsible for them.
- **Young candidates:** they may not have had the chance to create results, so evaluate potential. The primary attributes are intelligence and the ability to learn quickly.
- Drive and passion matter too: "hard work makes up for a lot."

chunks.heading: Interviewing is rolling the dice, and gut feel improves with practice
chunks.text:
- "When you recruit, you're rolling the dice." He gets at most an hour with a candidate and still has to recommend hire or no hire. Others recommend too, so he is one vote among several.
- Ultimately it "comes down to your gut feeling."
- The gut gets refined by tracking outcomes. When someone he expected to do well doesn't, he asks what he overlooked. When someone he doubted succeeds, he asks why.
- Over time, "your gut instinct gets better and more precise," and so does his digging in interviews.

chunks.heading: Testing candidates under pressure: provoke them on purpose
chunks.text:
- He researches what the candidate worked on, then deliberately criticizes it: "That really turned out to be a bomb. That really turned out to be a bozo product. Why did you work on that?"
- "The worst thing that someone can do in an interview is to agree with me and knuckle under."
- He wants someone to come back with "You're dead wrong and here's why." The goal is to see whether they fold or show firm conviction, belief and pride in their work.
- He sometimes tries to really anger a candidate to see the reaction.
- Reason: a company that is a meritocracy of ideas, full of passionate people, has "a lot of arguments." People who cannot argue well under pressure may not thrive there.

chunks.heading: Strengths and weaknesses are two sides of the same coin
chunks.text:
- Steve says he doesn't know his management weaknesses in the abstract: "People are package deals; you take the good with the confused."
- Strengths and weaknesses are "almost always the same thing." A strength in one situation is a weakness in another, and people often can't switch gears.
- **His strengths:** viewing technology "from a liberal arts perspective, from a human culture perspective," and being "a pretty good judge of people" who can bring them together around a common vision.
- **Liberal arts example:** Mac desktop publishing (proportionately spaced fonts, ease of use) "comes from books: the typography, that rich feel that nobody in computers knew anything about."
- **His weakness:** being too idealistic. "Sometimes best is the enemy of better." He sometimes goes for "best" when he should go for "better" and ends up "going nowhere or backwards."
- He can be blinded by "what could be" versus "what is possible," and by one fell swoop versus incremental change. Balancing the ideal and the practical is something he says he must keep paying attention to.

chunks.heading: Motivation: the work binds people, not charisma
chunks.text:
- "Ultimately, it's the work that motivates people. I sometimes wish it were me, but it's not." His job is to make sure the work is as good as it should be and to get people to stretch beyond their best.
- He doesn't credit charisma for the Macintosh team's output. Part of the CEO's job is "to cajole and beg and plead and threaten at times" to get people to see things in a bigger way and do better work than they thought they could.
- When people do their best and it isn't enough, tell them straight: "This isn't good enough. I know you can do better. You need to do better. Now go do better."
- Use that card carefully: "You must be right a lot of the time because you're messing with people's lives."

chunks.heading: Why the Mac team stayed bound: a product worth the sacrifice
chunks.text:
- A dozen years after shipping, most of the Macintosh team still say it was the most meaningful experience of their lives.
- That only holds because the product shipped and was good. "It wasn't just about going to camp with a bunch of fun people. It wasn't just a motivational speaker."
- The product expressed everyone's heart and soul and their "deep appreciation, somehow, for the world to see."
- "In the end, it's the work that binds." The environment, coworkers and work create the bond.
- So pick important things to do: "it's very hard to get people motivated to make a breakfast cereal. It takes something that's worth doing."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jobs recounts, in a 2003 Stanford talk, how he reluctantly came back to Apple and decided to act as permanent CEO from day one. His August 1997 email shows the first reset: focus on two markets, equity for everyone, shared sacrifice by executives, and consolidated teams.

chunks.heading: Why Steve returned to Apple, and how he reset it
chunks.text:
Steve sold NeXT to Apple only because a NeXT colleague pushed past his objections. He says "when you hire the right people, they don't always listen to you in key moments in time." The colleague raised the deal twice after Steve dismissed it, and Steve finally agreed to talk. Afterward he stayed on as a consultant to help the NeXT team avoid being "totally crushed" by Apple's weaker management.

- Steve says the NeXT management team was "actually quite a bit better" than the one Apple had.
- He was nearly out of the picture until an Apple board member he had never met asked for his honest view of the CEO. He decided to tell the truth because Apple was a company he had started and loved, even though it might cost him.
- Months later the director called to say the board would dismiss the CEO and wanted Steve to run the company.

chunks.heading: How Steve decided to come back (and the one-line test that settled it)
chunks.text:
- Steve first refused. He was CEO of Pixar, a public company, and felt he could not desert its employees and shareholders.
- The board then asked him to be interim leader while they found a new CEO. He was still unsure.
- He called a friend at another company to talk it through. After about four minutes the friend interrupted: "Steve, I don't give a shit about Apple. Why are you telling me all this?"
- Steve hung up and realized: "I do give a shit about Apple." That crystallized the decision.
- He returned as interim CEO, terrified that Pixar's people would feel deserted, and planned to stay about ninety days.

chunks.heading: Acting like the permanent CEO of a company in intensive care
chunks.text:
- The CEO candidates Apple was attracting were "not so good." Steve almost hired one and backed out at the last minute: "I can't do this to these guys."
- Ninety more days to find someone turned into a year.
- He decided up front to act as if he were the permanent CEO, because "they didn't need a caretaker."
- His description of Apple then: "in intensive care," about ninety days from bankruptcy.
- His view on CEOs: "you need a license to drive a car, but you don't need a license to be the CEO of a company. And maybe you should need one."

chunks.heading: August 1997: the first decisive steps toward renewal
chunks.text:
In an August 12, 1997 email, "A More Entrepreneurial Apple," Steve (not yet CEO) framed renewal as a journey. The first four weeks had brought:

- A new Board of Directors.
- A new product strategy and product roadmap.
- A decision to focus on two market segments: education and creative content.
- A new advertising agency.
- A détente and working partnership with Microsoft, announced at MacWorld the previous week.

The next steps aimed to take Apple "back to its roots as a more egalitarian, entrepreneurial company."

chunks.heading: Stock options as egalitarian ownership
chunks.text:
- Stock options became the primary form of "beyond-salary" compensation. Steve calls them egalitarian: when anyone's stock goes up $1 per share, everyone's does.
- The aim was for employees to be rewarded as public shareholders are, through stock appreciation, and to have a true stake in the company's future.
- The Executive Team gave up its current and future cash bonus plans in exchange for more options, to "lead the way."
- All existing options were repriced to $13.25 on July 11. On August 5 the board approved new grants of six million shares at $19.75.
- Apple had granted options on over 10 million shares since the start of the calendar year. Employees held options on over 20 million shares, more than 16% of outstanding shares. Steve calls that very high for a company of Apple's size and comparable to many Valley start-ups.
- His framing: public shareholders and employee option holders all benefit "in harmony" as Apple's fortunes are restored.

chunks.heading: One severance plan, one travel policy, no sabbaticals
chunks.text:
- **Severance:** a single plan for all employees replaced the separate executive plan. It gives a 60-day notice period with full pay and benefits, plus one additional week of severance pay per full year of service. For example, three to four years of service means three weeks of severance.
- **Sabbaticals:** discontinued at the end of the fiscal year because "Apple needs all hands on deck." Employees who earned one by September 26, 1997 could take it during fiscal 1998.
- **Travel:** limited to essential trips. The "egalitarian" policy is coach for everyone on trips under 10 hours and business class for everyone on trips of 10 hours or more. Employees may upgrade with personal funds or mileage, and San Francisco to Tokyo flights qualify for business class.

chunks.heading: Consolidating facilities for "beehive" effects
chunks.text:
- Steve moved as many employees as possible onto the R&D Campus.
- The goal was the "beehive" effect: faster communication paths and more unplanned interactions between groups.
- The R&D Campus was renamed the Apple Campus.
- He signed the email "Steve and the Executive Team," presenting the changes as a shared effort.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 1997 email exchange, Avie Tevanian argues Apple's culture is a recurring "cancer" and floats selling the company. Jobs agrees employees dodge responsibility for bad products, marketing and support, but insists Apple is worth saving as the only alternative to Windows. He also asks Avie to keep challenging him, because disagreement is how the team reaches the right decisions.

chunks.heading: Steve's reaction to Avie's "sell the company" email: Apple is worth saving
chunks.text:
When Avie Tevanian (ran software engineering at NeXT, then at Apple) said the bad Apple culture was returning and suggested it might be time to sell the company, Steve answered the same night, August 14, 1997. He said he had felt the same way lately: that Apple employees "don't deserve to be saved."

- Steve's complaint was about missing accountability. Employees "think they work so hard", but he does not see it.
- They also "think they have no responsibility for any of the mess that Apple's in."
- He lists who made the mess: the people who "engineered and shipped such bad products," who "created and authorized such bad marketing," and who "caused the support to be so bad."
- He says they "just don't want to share any responsibility for the current state of the company."

chunks.heading: Why Steve still thought Apple was worth saving
chunks.text:
Steve did not accept selling the company, even after agreeing with Avie's low opinion of the employees. He wrote: "there is something good here worth saving."

- He admitted he could not fully express it: "I don't quite know how to express it."
- His reason was strategic. Apple is "the ONLY alternative to Windows."
- He argued Apple "can still inject some new thinking into the equation."
- The case for saving the company rested on what Apple could still contribute to the industry. He did not argue that the people deserved saving.

chunks.heading: Separating the mission from the people who work there
chunks.text:
The exchange shows Steve holding two views at once during the 1997 turnaround.

- He judged Apple's employees harshly, as a group that would not own the company's failures in products, marketing and support.
- He still believed the company was worth saving, because it was the only real alternative to Windows.
- Avie made the same split. He said the company "isn't worth saving. At least not for the sake of the employees," while still feeling for customers, shareholders and the ex-NeXT people brought in.
- Steve treated bad culture as something to fix by acting, not a reason to give up. Avie described applying a "new chemo treatment" against the "cancer" and expected another wave of resignations.

chunks.heading: Steve on being challenged
chunks.text:
On August 25, 1997, Avie wrote that he was unmotivated and, for the first time in 10 years, no longer felt like challenging Steve's ideas when he disagreed. Avie said this scared him, because "as a 'team' we work best when we challenge each other and come out all-the-better for it."

- Steve replied in a single line, 21 minutes after the email: "Please continue to challenge me."
- His reasoning: "It's the way we get to the right decisions, and I enjoy it too."
- He treated disagreement from a trusted lieutenant as the way the team reaches good decisions, and said he enjoyed it.
- He wanted Avie's pushback back at a moment when Avie was close to giving up.

chunks.heading: How Steve handled a discouraged lieutenant
chunks.text:
Avie was worn down in August 1997. He described falling revenue, losing quarters, ongoing restructuring, resignations, and poor engineering reaction to the new sabbatical program, with threats of a "sick-out." Steve's responses in the exchange:

- He replied within about 30 minutes, the same evening.
- He agreed with the frustration without piling on.
- He gave a reason to keep going, which was Apple's unique role as the alternative to Windows.
- He proposed talking in person: "Let's go for a walk and talk about this sometime soon." Avie had also asked for a face-to-face, one-on-one conversation, not a phone call.
- He asked Avie to keep arguing with him, which kept the working relationship honest.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Weeks after returning to Apple, Jobs explains the turnaround: cut 70% of the product roadmap, simplify distribution, and rebuild the brand around values rather than specs. He introduces the "Think Different" campaign, citing Nike and "Got Milk?" as models of marketing that conveys who a company is, not what its product does.

chunks.heading: Back to basics: great products, great marketing, great distribution
chunks.text:
- Steve says that when he returned (about eight to ten weeks earlier), his aim was not "highfalutin": "We're trying to get back to the basics of great products, great marketing, and great distribution."
- His view: Apple "has pockets of greatness but in some ways has drifted away from doing the basics really well."
- The new "Think Different" ad was finished at three o'clock the night before he showed it to employees.

chunks.heading: Cutting the product line by 70 percent
chunks.text:
- Steve and the team reviewed the product road map for the next few years and concluded: "A lot of this doesn't make sense, and it's way too much stuff, and there's not enough focus."
- They cancelled 70 percent of the road map.
- He could not figure out the product line himself after a few weeks ("What is this model? How does this fit?"), and customers could not figure it out either.
- Result he promises: a product line that is "much simpler" and "much better", with more focus on the remaining 30 percent, the "gems", plus a few new things that take Apple in new directions.
- Engineers whose projects were cancelled left the meeting "three feet off the ground with excitement" because they finally understood where the company was going and liked the strategy.

chunks.heading: Taking inventory out of the pipeline
chunks.text:
- Apple held two to three months of inventory in its manufacturing supplier pipeline and about the same again in its distribution channel, forcing guesses four, five or six months ahead about what customers want.
- Steve's verdict: "We're not smart enough to do that. I don't think Einstein's smart enough to do that."
- Fix: get simple and take inventory out of both pipelines, so the customer tells Apple what they want and Apple can "respond to it super fast."
- Ambition: catch up with the best in distribution, then break new ground in distribution and manufacturing within the coming months.

chunks.heading: Marketing is about values, not specs
chunks.text:
- "To me, marketing is about values." The world is complicated and noisy, and no company gets people to remember much about it, so a company must be very clear about the one thing it wants them to know.
- Apple is one of "half-a-dozen best brands in the whole world", alongside Nike, Disney, Coke and Sony, but even a great brand "needs investment and caring if it's going to retain its relevance and vitality." Apple's had suffered neglect for a few years.
- Do not talk about "speeds and feeds", MIPS and megahertz, or why Apple is better than Windows.
- Apple spent a fortune on advertising: "You'd never know it."

chunks.heading: Lessons from Got Milk? and Nike
chunks.text:
- The dairy industry spent twenty years telling people milk was good for them, and sales fell. Steve says that claim is "a lie" but they tried anyway.
- "Got Milk?" reversed the trend, and it "doesn't even talk about the product"; the focus is on the absence of the product.
- Nike is "one of the greatest jobs of marketing that the universe has ever seen". It sells a commodity (shoes), yet people feel something beyond a shoe company.
- Its ads never discuss air soles or why they beat Reebok's. Instead Nike honors great athletes and great athletics: "That's who they are. That's what they are about."

chunks.heading: How the Think Different campaign came about
chunks.text:
- On arrival, Apple had just fired its agency and was running a competition among twenty-three agencies that would have picked a winner "four years from now". Steve blew it up and hired Chiat/Day, whom he had worked with before.
- That earlier work included "1984", voted the best ad ever made by advertising professionals.
- Work started about eight weeks before the speech. The question: customers want to know who Apple is, what it stands for and where it fits in the world.
- The campaign is Apple's first brand-marketing campaign in several years.

chunks.heading: Apple's core value: people with passion can change the world
chunks.text:
- Apple is not about "making boxes for people to get their jobs done", though it does that better than almost anybody.
- Core value: "We believe that people with passion can change the world for the better." Those crazy enough to think they can change the world "are the ones that actually do."
- Apple has worked with developers, customers and employees who have done it, in big and small ways.
- Market, products, distribution and manufacturing have all changed, "but values and core values: those things shouldn't change."
- "Think Different" honors people who changed the world, living or not; the ones who are gone "would have used a Mac" if they had used a computer. Steve: "It touches the soul of this company."
- The ad text he screens: "Here's to the crazy ones. The misfits. The rebels. The troublemakers. The round pegs in the square holes... About the only thing you can't do is ignore them. Because they change things. They push the human race forward... the people who are crazy enough to think they can change the world are the ones who do."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A set of internal emails from 1997 to 1999 showing Jobs holding teams accountable with honest letter grades, setting a short list of annual milestones to keep sight of the "forest", cutting products like Newton for focus, and celebrating wins by crediting the team. The Macintosh anniversary note restates Apple's purpose: bridge sophisticated technology and ordinary people, at the intersection of technology and liberal arts.

chunks.heading: Pixar year-end report card: grading 1997 against the plan
chunks.text:
In his December 21, 1997 email to Pixar's senior leadership, Steve graded the company against the milestones he had written down in October 1996.

- Four A's, one B, and two F's.
- "Make BUGS Great": A.
- "Ship Two Strong Interactive Products": F, but with an A "for getting out" of the interactive business.
- "Enter Sequel Business": A, "and almost exit sequel business."
- "Greenlight Film #3": F, but a B "for great progress."
- "Manage Growth": A. Pixar hired more than 100 people, started "Pixar U," and expanded its infrastructure.
- Long-term goals: keeping a larger percentage of the profits earned an A, and increasing Pixar's brand awareness earned a B, "mostly due to Apple goings on."
- He graded the work honestly and gave partial credit when an F came from a sensible decision to exit rather than a failure of effort.
- He set the next year's goals right after the holidays, so the grading led straight into planning.

chunks.heading: Keeping the "forest" in view: Pixar's 1998 milestones
chunks.text:
Steve proposed nine milestones for 1998 on December 26, 1997. He said the list existed "to remind us of the 'forest' from time to time, and to help prod us into taking corrective action when we get off track."

- A Bug's Life opens in November to "very strong critical and box office success."
- PR efforts win Pixar branding and creative credit for A Bug's Life.
- Toy Story 2 becomes "a great feature film."
- Hidden City, the film that became Monsters, Inc., begins animation by April 1998.
- Film #5 development begins by April 1.
- Emeryville groundbreaking happens in May.
- A "breakthrough new animation system" is demonstrated by summer.
- Shorts projects are secured to cover the carrying costs of the A Bug's Life crew through spring 1999.
- Equity financing is executed in spring or summer if necessary.
- The list mixes creative, brand, facilities, technology, and financing goals, and it has dates and checkable outcomes.
- He invited his team to "shoot full of holes" the list, so the plan was open to challenge.

chunks.heading: Handling the Newton protest: welcome the critics, stand by the decision
chunks.text:
On March 6, 1998, Steve emailed all Apple employees about a protest over the end of Newton OS development, especially the MessagePad. Newton was one of the product lines he cut after returning to Apple to focus the company's offerings.

- Newton customers and developers were coming to campus to protest.
- He told employees the protest was "OK."
- Apple reserved a space for the protesters and provided coffee and hot drinks, since it might be cold.
- The decision "was not taken lightly, and is unlikely to be reversed."
- He asked staff to welcome the protesters anyway.
- His hope was that they would feel Apple's enthusiasm about its future and "leave more settled than they arrived."
- He combined firmness on the decision with courtesy toward upset customers.

chunks.heading: Celebrating A Bug's Life: the record Thanksgiving weekend
chunks.text:
On November 30, 1998, Steve emailed Pixar with the box office results for A Bug's Life.

- It earned a record $46.5 million over the five-day Thanksgiving weekend, beating the previous record of $45 million set by Disney's live-action 101 Dalmatians in 1996.
- Its three-day (Friday to Sunday) take of $33.6 million was also a Thanksgiving record.
- Exit polls were "exceptionally positive."
- The audience was split equally between males and females.
- 16% of the audience was the non-family "date" audience, which Toy Story did not reach until two weeks after its opening.
- Competitors for the weekend: Rugrats took $27.6 million, Babe: Pig in the City $8.5 million, and Antz $1.2 million.
- He credited John, Andrew, Darla, Kevin, and the whole A Bug's Life crew, and also Jan, Karen, and the Geri's Game crew for the short.
- He turned the numbers into people: $46.5 million divided by an average ticket price of around $6 meant about 7.5 million people saw the film that weekend.
- In his words: "Few people ever get the chance to make 7.5 million people laugh so much and feel so good. Or 450 people at Pixar feel so proud."

chunks.heading: Telling Apple employees "We did it!": iMac at number one
chunks.text:
On December 23, 1998, Steve emailed Apple employees that the iMac had been the number one selling computer in the U.S. in November, in retail and mail order channels.

- iMac captured 7.1% of unit volume and 8.2% of dollar volume.
- Apple's overall retail and mail order market share doubled, from about 5% in August to 10% in November.
- The news ran on Apple's website and on pages A1 and B7 of the Wall Street Journal.
- He credited "our hard work" and asked employees to reflect on how far the company had come "in the last 18 months."
- He said he was proud of the team and excited to be at Apple.

chunks.heading: Macintosh at fifteen: Apple's job is to bridge technology and "the rest of us"
chunks.text:
On January 24, 1999, the fifteenth anniversary of the Macintosh launch at Flint Center, Steve wrote to Apple employees about Apple's purpose.

- The Mac's "revolutionary ease of use" made computing accessible to "the rest of us."
- Its graphics and typography put it "at the intersection of computer science and liberal arts."
- He called it the second revolution in personal computing, after the Apple II.
- He said he was "not normally one to look back," but that today was a good day to remember Apple's legacy.
- That legacy is to bridge "the gap between sophisticated technology and 'the rest of us' who make up most of humanity."
- "It's our job to make complex technology easy to use and fun to use."
- The need was greater than in 1984, because users now faced networks, the Internet, email setup, device drivers, and init files, "all of the other things that drive today's computer users mad."
- Computing was not getting simpler, and no other company had taken Apple's place as "the bridge builder."
- He described Apple's return to its roots as delivering "simpler and better ways to use computers," and said that made its future look "both bright and secure."
- His closing line: "It's been an amazing journey so far, yet we have barely begun."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: At Macworld, interim CEO Jobs borrows Maslow to explain Apple's turnaround as a ladder of skeptic questions: survival, stable business, product strategy, growth. He shows how cutting 15 platforms to four products let Apple put its A team on each, and why brand, design and simplicity drive growth.

chunks.heading: Survival came first, then stability: how Steve framed Apple's turnaround as the "Apple Hierarchy of Skepticism"
chunks.text:
- Steve borrowed Abraham Maslow's hierarchy of needs to build what he called the "Apple Hierarchy of Skepticism". Each time Apple convinced people it had solved one level of doubt, the critics moved up to the next.
- He stopped seeing this as a bad thing: "what it means is we've now convinced them that we've taken care of last month's question, and they're onto the next one." His advice was to get ahead of the game by mapping the questions in advance.
- The levels, in order, were survival, a stable business, product strategy, and growth.
- Level one, survival. A year earlier the refrain was "Apple is dying." Steve points to three things that changed minds: a new management team, a new board with phenomenally experienced people, and a deal with Microsoft. The largest software company in the world helping Apple "added a lot of credibility".
- Level two, a stable business. Apple delivered $47 million of profit in the first full quarter under the new team and $55 million in the next. A third consecutive profitable quarter was due to be announced a week later. Steve also cites rising retention ("hardly any" people leaving) and hiring "incredibly good people".
- Other stability moves: realigned distribution channels, the "Think Different" brand campaign plus specific product advertising, and an online store that had become one of the largest ecommerce sites on the internet. Apple's market value rose from about $1.8 billion a year earlier to about $4 billion the day before.

chunks.heading: Cutting to four products so the A team can work on every one
chunks.text:
- When Steve arrived, Apple had fifteen product platforms and "a zillion variants of each one". After about three weeks he asked, "How are we going to explain this to others when we don't even know which products to recommend to our friends?"
- He went "back to Business School 101" and asked what people want. The answer was two kinds of products, consumer and pro (design and publishing customers need pro), each in desktop and portable models. That makes four products.
- Steve's argument for four:
  - "We could put the A team on every single one of them."
  - They could turn each product every nine months instead of every eighteen.
  - They could work on the next generation or two of each product while introducing the first.
- The four: Power Mac G3 (pro desktop), PowerBook G3 (pro portable), the iMac (consumer desktop), and a consumer portable announced May 6th for the first half of the next year.

chunks.heading: The iMac: a consumer product Apple had lacked for years
chunks.text:
- Within his first month Steve saw that Apple was walking away from the consumer market. It had no compelling product under $2,000 and had not had one for some time.
- He started a program immediately "to build the most kickass consumer product we knew how to do".
- The goal for the iMac was to combine "the excitement of the internet with the simplicity of a Macintosh". He says it is gorgeous and believes it will change the way computers look and should look.
- He frames consumer as the main growth lever. Apple invented the market for selling computers to consumers, then failed for years to ship compelling products at consumer prices.
- The existing strongholds were design and publishing (Apple market share between 50 and 90 percent depending on the segment) and education (over half the installed base and about 35 percent of new unit sales, bigger than anyone else). Adding consumer would strengthen both.

chunks.heading: Design and fashion as the competitive edge as prices fall
chunks.text:
- Steve argues that as price points come down and the consumer market blossoms, design and fashion matter more.
- His example: the most popular watch in the world is popular because of its design, not because it tells time better. Ten years earlier the average American owned one watch; with design entering the market, the average American owned seven. "Seven watches because of design. Because of fashion."
- He calls Apple's in-house industrial design team the best he has seen in his life. The PowerBook G3 and iMac were designed inside Apple by "brilliant, brilliant, super hardworking people", and he promises "a continual stream of very innovative design out of Apple, I think the best in the industry by a mile."

chunks.heading: Brand as an asset that takes decades to build
chunks.text:
- Steve says no brand in the computer industry is remotely as strong as Apple's. He puts it alongside Disney, Sony and Nike in recognition and consumer loyalty.
- He notes those other three brands all had serious problems too (Disney when Michael Eisner arrived, Nike and Sony in the previous half-dozen years), and came back stronger once the problems were fixed.
- His conclusion: "Brands take decades to build. And we think we have one of the best in the world."

chunks.heading: Four assets behind the growth case
chunks.text:
- Steve names four "incredibly powerful, unique, compelling assets" for Apple's growth:
  - The brand.
  - The installed base, especially in consumer and education.
  - Design that can carry products into the consumer space of fashion.
  - Products that are dramatically simpler to set up and use than the competition's.
- He closes by returning to Maslow and saying Apple had demonstrated, step by step, that it was "coming back in a very big way."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Two 2000 pieces: a private email where Jobs distills Apple's reason for being (making high technology easy for "mere mortals"), and his speech opening Pixar's headquarters. The speech shows how a building should reflect a company's soul, built with craft, collaboration and iteration like its films.

chunks.heading: Apple's purpose: making high technology easy for "mere mortals"
chunks.text:
- Steve's private note (Oct 29, 2000) defines Apple as "the world's premier company at building high technology products that are easy to learn and use by mere mortals."
- The motive is love for what personal computers can do to "enhance and enrich the lives of regular people", not just spreadsheets and databases but creative uses.
- Apple "marries state of the art technology with Apple's legendary ease-of-use."
- He keeps rewording the idea. The final version: Apple is the premier company at making the exploding world of high technology easy to learn and use, so mere mortals can enrich their lives with it.
- He calls Apple "the world's premier bridge builder between mere mortals and the exploding world of high technology."
- Apple has set the standard for easy-to-use systems and software for over 20 years.

chunks.heading: Apple as a creatively driven company
chunks.text:
- Steve calls Apple "a creatively driven company in everything we do": breakthrough features, operating systems, culturally leading product design, and advertising.
- His proof points: "we INVENTED the personal computer, spawned desktop publishing and are now bringing desktop movies to millions."
- He notes engineers were working on more breakthroughs due in 2001.
- Creativity is the identity, and technology is the means.

chunks.heading: Demystified technology and the purpose of the stores
chunks.text:
